Luctifico fratrem plenus amore dolet.
At tu Spirenses Erneste profecte penates,
Externo fratris fata sub axe gemis.
Utque sequebaris nuper pia Saxonis arma,
Coniunctis pugnax uiribus: Hesse tuis.
Interea fratrem cui gracia nomen, iniquo
Crudelis raperet funere parca domi.
Cesare concilium sic nunc quoque agente, salutem
Quod precor et pacem munera grata ferat.
Cum duce Saxonie teque hoc uisente, Philippum
Amittis simili nunc ratione domi.
Ergo graues merito lachrymas Erneste profundis,
Quodque fleas causa est iusta grauisque tibi.
Vos etiam gnati tristes de morte parentis,
Fletis, habetque grauis pectora uestra dolor.
Iusta parit uobis ingentes causa querelas,
Quas carpens uera nil rationis habet.
Hactenus extinctam matrem patruumque Iohannem
Fleuistis, fletis cum patre utrosque modo.
Arxque suo tristis nunc utraque luget adempto
Patre, suas lachrymis Oraque miscet aquas.
Quid multis opus est, sunt omnia plena doloris,
Quodque fleat merito subditus omnis habet.
Nos quoque qui colimus uicini littora VVcite,
Te querula flemus clare Philippe cheli.
Flemus et hisce tuae canimus praeconia laudis
Versibus, inculti sint licet atque rudes.

At the time when the Prince of Saxony, and Philipp,
The leader and father of the Hessian soil,
Were taking up arms against the Tyrant of Brunswick,
And the army was about to set out.
As the stone <note>kidney or bladder stone</note> had severely tormented me before,
And there was no hope of recovering health.
I was ordering this to be cut out by medical art,
Since the one who was greater was already born.
I send this immediately to Gotha to be seen by my brother,
Who was then the standard-bearer of the Saxon sword.
Having seen it, wondering at the weight of the deadly stone,
He returned such sounds with prophetic mouth.
Surely this is a sign of death, dearest brother,
It teaches you that you will soon yield to the living.
From here, therefore, after Phoebus had made the third triple rising <note>nine days later</note>,
We closed the day in the final circle.

### XV.

In which way, indeed, we willingly admit that universals are everywhere and always, not indeed that they themselves subsist by themselves, or in their individuals, everywhere and always: but that by their nature they are not concluded in any certain place or defined time. For they have this restriction from their individuals, which if they could be everywhere and always, then the universals themselves would also be always and everywhere.

### XVI.

Nor does this take away their perpetual truth from certain propositions, which express to us either the essences of things, or the affections of essences: since they are not considered necessary because the things signified by them have always existed, or will exist, but because their verb signifies not existence, but only a certain connection of the attribute with the subject, which some more recent <term>Dialecticians</term> <gloss>logicians</gloss> have been accustomed to call the absolution of the verb from time.

### XVII.

Nor do we overturn any certainty of the disciplines by this pact: but rather, against <term>Heraclitus</term> <gloss>Greek philosopher</gloss> and <term>Cratylus</term> <gloss>Greek philosopher</gloss>

Aceruatim iam reliqua iudices dicam, ut ad ea, quae propiora huius causae, et adiunctiora sunt, perueniam. uos quaeso memoria teneatis, non mihi hoc esse propositum, ut accusem Oppianicum mortuum, sed, cum hoc persuadere uobis uelim, iudicium ab hoc non esse corruptum, hoc uti initio ac fundamento defensionis, Oppianicum, hominem sceleratissimum, et nocentissimum, esse damnatum: qui uxori suae Cluentiae, quae amita huius Habiti fuit, cum ipse poculum dedisset, subito illa in media potione exclamauit, se maximo cum dolore mori, nec diutius uixit, quam locuta est: nam in ipso sermone hoc, et uociferatione mortua est. et ad hanc mortem tam repentinam, uocemque morientis omnia praeterea, quae solent esse indicia, et uestigia ueneni, in illius mortuae corpore fuerunt: eodemque ueneno C. Oppianicum fratrem necauit. neque est hoc satis: tametsi in ipso fraterno parricidio nullum scelus praetermissum uidetur: tamen, ut ad hoc nefarium facinus accederet, aditum sibi aliis sceleribus ante muniuit: nam cum esset grauida Auria fratris uxor, et iam appropinquare partus uideretur, mulierem ueneno interfecit, ut una illa,

seed: and by pity for that young man. Therefore, when A. Aurius, who had previously denounced him, began to pursue the man with shouting and threats, he fled from Larinum and betook himself to the camp of the most illustrious man, Q. Metellus. After that flight, he, the witness of both his crime and his guilty conscience, never dared to entrust himself to trials, never to the laws, never unarmed, to his enemies: but through that force and victory of L. Sulla, he swooped into Larinum in the great fear of all with armed men. He removed the four men <note>the <term>Quattuorviri</term>, local magistrates</note> whom the townspeople had made: he said that he and three others besides had been made magistrates by Sulla, and that he had been ordered by him to take care that that Aurius, who had threatened him with the laying of a name and danger to his head, and the other Aurius, and his son Gaius, and Sex. Virbius, who was said to have been used as a middleman in the bribing of that informer, were to be proscribed and killed. And so, with them most cruelly killed, the rest were terrified by no small fear of proscription and death from him. With these things brought to light in the case and the trial, who is there who would think that he could have been acquitted? And these things are small: learn the rest, so that you may wonder not that Oppianicus was finally convicted, but that he remained safe for so long. First, see the audacity of the man. He coveted to take into marriage Sassia, the mother of Habitus, that woman whose husband, A. Aurius, he had killed. Whether he is more impudent for asking, or she more cruel for marrying him, is difficult to say. But nevertheless, learn the decency and steadfastness of both. Oppianicus asks that Sassia marry him, and he struggles greatly for it. She, however, does not wonder at his audacity, does not despise his impudence, nor, finally, does she dread that right hand of Oppianicus dripping with her husband’s blood: but she answered that she shrunk from these nuptials because he had three sons. ### XXXIV
A public convention is that which is made through peace, as often as military commanders agree on certain things among themselves, <term>law 5</term> below, Digest concerning agreements.

### XXXV
Yet, not every public convention is to be called peace, which seemed to be gathered from the words of <term>Ulpian</term>, but they stand in relation to each other as genus and species; for instance, so that a public convention might include peace as a species.

### XXXVI
For agreements are made also for the sake of truces, as well as for the ransoming of captives, the undertaking of battle, and similar things, which are carried out on the occasion of war, according to the situation, just as treaties are sometimes made without the occasion of war.

### XXXVII
And here it is greatly debated: can a Prince, while making peace with an enemy, remit the damages inflicted upon his subjects? This does not seem permissible, unless those damages are compensated either by the contribution of the other citizens or from the treasury of the Prince, by the argument of <term>law 13, paragraph 1</term>, Digest concerning common estates, and <term>law 2</term>, Code concerning the causes for which servants receive liberty for a reward.

### XXXVIII
A private convention is said to be that which is made regarding the private affairs of individuals, <term>Wesenbecius</term> in the verse Digest concerning agreements number 4, or which pertains to the private matters of private persons.

### XXXIX
Its species are two: the pact called in particular, and the contract.

Sed quis tamen tam facile crediderit, tantum Virum, in tanta dignitate ac auctoritate apud Romanos eque ac Judaeos constitutum, sese eo usque submisisse, ut munus hoc, quod militibus ac lictoribus velut proprium expediendum erat, ipse exequeretur? Haud itaque est absurdum, sed valde commodum, verba Evangelistarum sic exponere. XXVII. Insuper ministerialem causam indagantes, non abs re judicamus quaerere, quinam ac quales ad JESUM flagellandum praecipue sint admissi? Hic si intuemur Grecos emendatiores codices, non invenimus in textu separatim, quoad hoc, mentionem eorum fieri: colligimus tamen non male ex verbis, tum antecedentibus, tum consequentibus, Romanos milites & lictores, ab aliquibus Brutianos vel Brutios dictos, eosque gentiles, praecipuos fuisse hujus tragoediae actores. Nam adjecta & Judaeos respiciens vocula, *Eis*, quae in exemplaribus quibusdam post vocem, *tradidit*, legitur, non est genuina: hinc, ERASMO notante, nonnihil officit sensui.

Neque enim (addit is) Judaeis tradidit JESUM Pilatus, sed suis militibus, supplicii ministris. Hi siquidem et ipsi Christum antea ceperunt, captum vinxerunt, vinctum judicii stiterunt, statum flagellarunt, flagellatum post purpura vestierunt, vestitum coronarunt, coronatum illuserunt, illusum verberarunt, verberatum abduxerunt, abductum crucifixerunt: sicuti id in historia totius passionis non semel, sed saepius, inculcari cernimus.

XXVIII. At dubium forsan alicui oriri posset, annon Judaei auxiliatrices suas hoc in negotio Ethnicis porrexerint manus? Certe, Juda proditore facem praeferente, hi ii tradiderunt Christum, nil aliud expetentes, quam ut e medio suo JESUS a gentilibus, post varios cruciatus, in crucem denique ipsam tolleretur. Quapropter culpam longe maximam integrae passionis, adeoque et flagellationis, in Judaeos, tanquam causas moraliter efficientes, inde redundare, quis nostrum unquam dubitat? Enimvero quod Judaei physicae cujusdam causae vicem in ullo opere obierint, nec legimus, nec credimus: cumprimis cum ipse patienter passus SERVATOR in ultimo itinere Hierosolymitano id ita discipulis suis de seipso praedixerit, futurum, ut Filium hominis Sacerdotum Principes ac Scribae tradant gentibus ad illudendum et εἰς μαστιγῶσαι ad flagellandum. Confer, MARC. & LUC. Videbis utrobique de gentibus, sive (quod in hisce aliisve plurimis locis idem) gentilibus, minime vero Judaeis, enunciari: μαστιγώσουσιν & μαστιγώσαντες αὐτόν. Unde ut impleretur simul veracissima haec VERITATIS praedictio, gentiles soli JESUM flagellare debebant.

XXX. Sed quid? Quâ tandem de causâ illud ab illis sit factum, scire nostrâ parùm refert. Revertimur rectiùs ad ipsum flagellandi actum. Collegimus antè ex Scripturae textu, immitibus potissimùm militibus satellitibusque Pilati à Pilato demandatum fuisse, ut flagellarent Jesum. Quot autem lictores illi praecisè fuerint, non diximus, nec dicere possumus; tacente praeprimis Scripturâ & antiquitate. Extra tamen controversiam plures uno, imò multi, si non plurimi, huic actui interfuerunt, qui ope operâque suâ flagellationis negotium adjuverunt. Locus, ubi flagellatio erat instituenda, statuebatur *atrium seu praetorium, domus, in quâ provincialis Praetor non habitabat modò, sed & jus dictitabat*. Eò enim Praesidis sese receperant milites, convocatâ simul ac congregatâ in illam universâ cohorte.

<margin>

</margin>

XXXI. Ibi verò fata flagellandorum singula Jesus experiri cogebatur. *Vestibus eundem fuisse privatum*, cur hic negabimus, qui audivimus superiùs, morem hunc in hâc inflictione poenarum Romanis *usitatissimum* mansisse? Praestamus etiam haud illibenter fidei nonnihil sententiae ei, quâ Jesum *columnae alligatum esse* asseritur; non tam proptereà, quòd *Lipsius* exemplis quibusdam ac testimoniis alienis ritum hunc studuerit confirmare, quàm quòd pii ipsi & in religione antiqui Patres non planè dubitârint tale quid de columnâ flagellati Servatoris adstruere. Clarè ac praeclarè prudentissimus Poëtarum suo adhuc seculo cecinit:

Hieronymus de Paula* in ejus Epitaphio ad *Eustochium* recitat: *Ostendebatur, inquiens, illi in monte Sion columna porticum sustinens, infecta cruore Domini, ad quam dicitur vinctus & flagellatus.* Tempore *Bedae* in medio Ecclesiae fuisse ipse Beda testatur. Sed quod de columnâ hâc in templo positâ dicitur, haud immeritò suspectum minimùm, si non penitus falsum, esse censemus. Interim sive extiterit, sive non, in templo columna talis, sufficit extitisse in praetorio tum, cùm ad eam Christus vinciretur. Hinc *Hieron. For even with *Beza* confessing on chapter 27 of *Matthew* that there is one flagellation, not a double one, it is clear from the circumstances. It was not, therefore, in reality different, even if it is described in different ways by different Evangelists: since *Matthew* and *Mark* placed the sentence of crucifixion pronounced by *Pilate* before the flagellation, thus not observing the order of deeds (as Evangelists are often accustomed to anticipate in their Gospels), which *John*, however, had correctly and properly observed here: whence he seems to have noted the circumstances here a little more distinctly and clearly than they.

<margin>Luke 23, verse 26.</margin>
XXIII. Namely, the matter stood thus. When *Pilate* had noticed that he had completely failed in his hope of freeing JESUS from death due to the option of the people, who preferred the robber *Barabbas* to be left alive rather than the most precious ransom, CHRIST: then he apprehended that medium still, and by apprehending JESUS, he adjudged the same to the scourges. With this judgment having been made, he labored to appease the fury of the Jews again, having trusted that thus, after these scourges had been inflicted, the Jews, moved by mercy, might at last pronounce the wretched JESUS free from the death of the cross. For the same reason, it is read in LUKE that he brought forth these words to the Jews: *Therefore I will release him after he has been chastised*.

XXIV. From which it follows of its own accord that Christ was subjected to scourges in a different manner than had been customary to be done otherwise. For the cause in itself was not going to be the affliction and affixing of the cross; for this *Pilate*, as much as he could, was still attempting to ward off from JESUS, whom he himself had sensed to be an innocent man. But that punishment was applied only as a medium, by which the Ethnic Praetor had sought to satisfy the cruelty of the Jews to a certain extent, although in vain (as the outcome taught).

<margin>book 3 of Sacred Philology, Treatise 7, Canon 13, p. 825 et seqq.</margin>
XXV. As this explanation of ours agrees precisely with the continuous narrative of JOHN, it is so far from differing in reality from the description of the other two, although it might appear to, that they rather agree with us entirely; if only the single particle, ἵνα <gloss>that</gloss>, is explained and understood in the way it ought to be here. For as it is indeed well known, this causal conjunction does not always and everywhere import a cause, but more often denotes only an outcome and a consequence; just as, besides this, other examples can be given, many of which the Blessed GLASSIUS has collected. Naturally, with the Jews urging too much, the lifting onto the cross did indeed follow the flagellation, but only as a result: for beyond the first intention of *Pilate*, which he had cherished, the execution of the cross then followed. Indeed, if we observe the order of the words of *Matthew*, the Greek context itself teaches that the matter coheres so well that it is said first that *Pilate* scourged JESUS, and afterward it is added that he handed him over so that he might be crucified. By which itself is hinted at the very different action of *Pilate*: for he seems to have been one thing while he was scourging Christ, and clearly another when he had handed him over to be crucified.

Hinc duplici vice **JESUM** flagra sustinuisse aliqui volunt: quos inter numerandi *Gerson, Arias Montanus, Montacutius*. Nihilominus non *bis*, sed *semel* tantummodò, flagellatum esse **JESUM** nostrum, omnium probabilissimè nos cum S. Ecclesiae Patre defendimus. 

<margin>l. 3. de Consensu Evangelistarum, c. 9.</margin>
Nam & *Beza* fatente ad c. 27. *Matth.* unam esse flagellationem, non duplicem, ex circumstantiis liquet. Non itaque ea reverà fuit diversa, etsi diversimodè â diversis Evangelistis sit descripta: quandoquidem *Matthaeus* ac *Marcus* flagellationi praeposuerunt prolatam *Pilati* de crucifixione sententiam, ordinem adeò factorum (ceu saepiùs solent in Evangeliis suis anticipare Evangelistae) non observantes, quem tamen rectè ac ritè hîc observaverat *Johannes*: Unde & paulò distinctiùs ac dilucidiùs hic prae illis annotasse circumstantias videtur.

<margin>Luc. 23. v. 26.</margin>
**XXIII.** Scilicet res ita se habuit. Cùm advertisset *Pilatus*, se spe suâ de liberando â nece **JESU** prorsus excidisse ob optionem populi, qui latronem *Barabbam* maluit vivum relinqui, quàm pretiosissimum λύτρον, **CHRISTUM**: tùm medium apprehendit adhuc illud, ipsumque prehendendo **JESUM** flagellis eundem adjudicavit. Quo quidem judicio facto, Judaeorum furorem denuò sedare laborabat, fore sic confisus, ut, post flagra haec inflicta, Judaei moti misericordiâ miserum **JESUM** â crucis morte liberum tandem pronunciarent. Eâdem enim de causâ apud **LUCAM** legitur hac ad Judaeos protulisse verba: *παιδεύσας οὖν αὐτὸν ἀπολύσω*, Castigatum ergò eum dimittam.

**XXIV.** Ex quo sponte suâ sequitur, Christum aliâ quâdam ratione, quàm aliàs fieri consveverat, flagellis fuisse subjectum. Causa namque per se non erat secutura crucis afflictio ac affixio; quippe hanc *Pilatus*, quantum poterat, tùm adhuc temporis â **JESU**, quem innocentem esse hominem ipse senserat, conabatur depellere. Sed adhibitum id est supplicium tantùm, tanquam medium, quo Praetor Ethnicus Judaeorum crudelitatem quaesiverat quadantenus, quanquam frustra, (ut eventus docuit) satiare.

<margin>l. 3. Philol sacr. Tract. 7. Canon. 13. p. m. 825. seqq.</margin>
**XXV.** Haec nostra explicatio uti cum continuâ **JOHANNIS** narratione ad amussim convenit: ita tantum abest, ut reapse â descriptione caeterorum duorum, quamvis videatur, discrepet, ut potiùs ipsi nobiscum ex asse consentiant; si unica modò particula, ἵνα, eo hîc, quo debet, modo explicetur atque intelligatur. Siquidem, ut utique notum est, causalis haec conjunctio non semper & ubiquè aliquam importat causam, sed eventum saepius ac sequelam tantùm denotat; quemadmodum praeter hoc exempla alia dari possunt, quorum multa collegit B. **GLASSIUS**. Nimirum nimiùm urgentibus Judaeis, flagellationem subsecuta quidem est in crucem elatio, sed ex eventu duntaxat: praeter primam enim *Pilati*, quam foverat, intentionem crucis executio deinde accesit. Imò si ordinem verborum *Matthaei* servemus, ipse contextus Graecus edocet, cohaerere rem sic optimè, ut primò *Pilatus* flagellâsse **JESUM** dicatur, posteà addatur demum, tradidisse, ut crucifigeretur. Quo ipso nonnihil innuitur diversissima *Pilati* actio: alia namque fuisse se videtur, dum flagellaret Christum; alia planè, cùm ad crucifigendum eundem tradidisset.

<margin>

</margin>

XXXII. Caetera, quae de hac columna traduntur, mira mere falsa ac ficta videntur. Nos ad propositum redimus, quod eo nunc revocat, ut lustremus instrumenta, quibus CHRISTI latera caesa fuerunt scissaque. Ac virgas quidem fuisse arbitratur *Erasmus*, nec abnuit *Maldonatus*. *Beza* tamen flagellis proprie dictis Christum percussum esse non male contendit; nec absque ratione: praeprimis quia in fonte voces μαστιγῶν ac φραγελλῶν ponuntur; quae significatione sua primaria id significant, quod propriissime flagellare dicitur. Ut adeo non necesse sit, praeter necessitatem a propria verborum significatione hic recedere. Facit huc, quod & *Nonnus* vocabula ἱμασθλης utatur, qua loreum denotatur flagellum. Narratur inter alia quoque; (an vere, alii videant) flagellis aculeatis, infixis aculeis & retractis, non evellendo sed sulcando, totum corpus Christi fuisse laceratum. Sane probabile alias est, pro Romano more, quem supra innuimus, militum saevitiam flagellis quoque aculeos adjecisse.

XXXIII. Quod si traditionibus credendum, (quibus tamen caute ac cum prudentia decet credere) tradunt aliqui, tribus flagellorum generibus Christum fuisse afflictum: primo vepribus & spinis acutissimis, post flagellis aculeatis, tandem ferreis catenulis. Verum quod attinet flagellum quo *Papicolae Romani* in aede B. Virginis Romae jam superbiunt, nos tanto non dignamur honore, ut sentiamus, illud iis esse accensendum, quibus dudum revera JESUS in praetorio sit casus. Mirum ni Pontificii post tot secula tales reliquias non adulterinas demum sartas tectas acceperint. Imo vero maxime mirum. Scilicet tanta ii prae nobis gaudent felicitate, si fas est credere. Sed gaudeant, ut ferme insaniant: nos pergimus ad reliqua dicenda.

<margin>
p. 1904.
</margin>

XXXIV. Nonnulli nimis fere curiosi sunt in eo, ut una cum aliis certum plagarum numerum inquirere haud supersederent. Ajunt enim *Brigittae* revelatum, CHRISTUM esse perpessum ultra quingenta millia ictuum ex flagellis. *Vincentius* in serm. de Passione colligit, cum ossa corporis ex sententia Medicorum sint ducenta sex & septuaginta, CHRISTUM ita fuisse flagellatum, ut cuilibet corporis ossi triplex verberum ictus responderet. *Gerson* numerum constantem allaturus: Dicunt aliqui, scribit, revelatum fuisse, quod Christus in corpore suo quingenta millia trecenta & septuaginta quinque acceperit plagarum. Vid. Harm. B. GERHARDI. Utut vero se res habeat cum hisce relationibus aut revelationibus, quas autorum suorum fidei merito relinquimus; certum tamen verberum definire numerum non solumus, nec possumus. Cum enim Romani non aeque, ut Judaei, definitas in flagellando infligerent plagas, quis, quaeso, facile credet, ab atrocibus istis militibus ea tum, quae Jesu dederant, numerata fuisse verbera? Numeraverint autem necne, temere certe fit, ignotum ictuum numerum nimium scrutari aut determinare velle, ex ejusmodi praesertim scriptis ac scriptoribus, qui valde dubiae sunt auctoritatis.

<margin>
in Harm. Evangel. p. 1905.
</margin>

XXXV. Sat est, si dixerimus, durissimam ac durissimam hanc SERVATORIS extitisse flagellationem. Colligitur id ut brevibus multa complectamur, satis ex textu circumstantiis. Nec obstant objectionculae duae, quas una cum Responsionibus B. Gerhardus adfert. Nos nostrae Dissertationi imponimus finem, ea, quae de ritu flagellandi supersunt exponenda, alio cum DEO, die proposituri. Jam quae restant, debitae sunt piaeque gratiae, quas Servatori nostro, pro flagitiosis nobis tantopere flagellato, dicere decet aeternum absque;

Pro remissiore autem fermentationis gradu, aeger illius molestias non sentit. 

Proclivitas ad somnum effectus quoque est viscositatis, crassitiei et penuriae spirituum animalium, caeterorumque liquorum, vel etiam compressionis cerebri. Non tamen Somnolentia inseparabile <term>Hemicraniae</term> est attributum, uti antea laudatus Piso innuere videtur. Sed vigiliae nimiae aliàs urgent, idque ob dolorum atrocitatem. Sudor contingit frigidus, quatenus glandulosus in superficie corporis contextus et tonus nimis est relaxatus, unde sero, qua data porta, facilis patet exitus; idemque frigidus est, ubi humores et praecipue sanguis, tum ob partes solidas, quas inter primatum cor obtinet, a motu constrictorio remittentes, adeo tarde canaliculos transeunt, ita ut agitationem istam, quae menti calorem repraesentat, producere non valeant. Vitiato genere nervoso, vitiatis etiam humoribus, quid boni sperabimus de ventriculo? Appetitus est progenies spirituum animalium, horum igitur usu denegato, suboritur nausea, quid? quod lympha gastrica corrupta non idonea sit ad cibos dissolvendos. Gravatus sic ventriculus jam satis debilis spasmodice sese contrahit, molemque indigestam iterum ejicit, quod <term>Vomitum</term> vocamus. Unde tumor in superficie capitis suas deducat natales, ex sectione antecedente petatur. Notandum insuper, non improbabile mihi videri, nonnunquam ejusmodi tumorem ab ipsa cranii carie ali posse.

X. With the investigation of causes completed thus far, I proceed to explain the syndrome of the *Symptoms*. Therefore, as far as the *lassitude of half the body* is concerned, it depends upon the influx of animal spirits into the nervous and muscular parts being denied, or upon sluggish spirits unfit for duly executing their function. If a certain acrimony is joined to these, the nervous fibers are eroded and lancinated, whence pain accompanies the lassitude. And just as all muscles are marked by this character in general, so it happens especially to the muscles of the thorax, so that they can no longer elevate the ribs; thus, the equilibrium between the pressing air and our body is necessarily destroyed, whence arises difficult respiration, with which anxiety of the precordia walks in equal step.

> *Often the sick do not dare to speak, and indeed are hardly able to, which must be deduced from the vehemence of the pains, or from a paralytic state of the organs dedicated to speech.*

> *Fever is present, insofar as the circulation of the humors, because of languid nerves and an abundance of morbific matter, does not succeed according to one's desire; hence it happens that they conceive a fermentation or intestinal motion.*

*A Dissertatio Inauguralis de Febre Maligna* [Inaugural Dissertation on Malignant Fever] by the most distinguished Licentiate J. C. WOLFF of Zerbst, formerly my most pleasant fellow student, held at Wittenberg under the most excellent Doctor BERGER, Public Professor there, that is to say, my venerable preceptor, will shed light on this opinion.

For a more remiss degree of fermentation, the sick person does not feel its disturbances.

A proclivity to sleep is also an effect of viscosity, thickness, and a shortage of animal spirits and other liquors, or even of compression of the brain. However, drowsiness is not an inseparable attribute of <term>Hemicrania</term>, as the aforementioned Piso seems to hint. But excessive vigils otherwise urge, and that on account of the atrocity of the pains. A cold sweat occurs, insofar as the glandular context and tone on the surface of the body is too relaxed, whence an easy exit for the serum is open by any given gate; and it is cold where the humors, and especially the blood, pass through the small canals so slowly that they cannot produce that agitation which represents heat to the mind, then on account of the solid parts, among which the heart holds primacy, relaxing from a constrictive motion. With the nervous genus corrupted, and the humors also corrupted, what good shall we hope for from the stomach? Appetite is the offspring of the animal spirits; therefore, with the use of these denied, nausea arises. What is more, the corrupted gastric lymph is not suitable for dissolving food. The stomach, thus burdened and now sufficiently weak, contracts itself spasmodically and ejects the indigested mass again, which we call <term>Vomiting</term>. Whence a tumor on the surface of the head derives its birth, let it be sought from the preceding section. It should be noted moreover that it does not seem improbable to me that such a tumor can sometimes be nourished by caries of the skull itself.

**XIII.** Videamus nunc, quænam morbus propositus ulterius portendat atque minetur, si prius monuerimus allatas §. præced. rationes fundamenti loco nobis inservire. Interni doloris non idem semper est eventus. Si liquor nerveus, vel ob materiæ, quâ constat, defectum, vel ob colatoriorum ejusdem obstructionem, deficiat, deficere quoque necesse est legitimum membrorum robur, & hinc vereor, ne ipsa Paralysis aut Hemiplegia jus suum cum tempore exercitura sit? Rationale est, laxatis lateris affecti musculis, habitum corporis imminere vitiatum, cùm alterius lateris quodammodo sani ab antagonistis derelicti musculi ad sua redeant principia & contrahantur. Quid oculis, quid auribus, quid linguæ, reliquisque sensuum organis ingruat damni, consideranti patet: Neque immerito metus nos subit, ne variorum inde viscerum oppilationes primordia sua capiant. X. Often, says Cicero, we speak verses in orations through imprudence, when we do not attend to or listen to ourselves. Whence it is clear that for the sake of this offense, it must be done at least by those who speak extemporaneously, not those who declaim from a paper.

XI. It is read that Demosthenes flashed and thundered: but he twisted his thunderbolts, as Quintilian testifies, with numbers <note>metrical feet</note>. These, therefore, when they have such power, and at the same time bind the oration with certain measures; let us close our sentences with numbers, lest our oration seem such as the motion of those whom the Greeks call unathletic <note>clumsy or lacking rhythm</note>.

XII. Logical abridgments are often wastes.

XIII. Not from the natural order of things, as Piccolomini wants, and Keckermann following him: but from our better and easier cognition, which is the truer opinion of Zabarella, whom many follow, the reason for ordering and arranging disciplines well and conveniently should be taken.

XIV. A definition is an oration: and although one word could express the whole nature of a thing: yet it is done confusedly, not distinctly, which finally happens when the same thing is explained by many words, each signifying its individual parts. Toletus, book 1, Intro. Dial. chapter 3, page 5, following.

XV. Although the ancient rite of covering new brides has been abolished, there are nonetheless weddings today: although they were called *nuptiae* <gloss>weddings</gloss> because the new bride was covered and veiled: nor does the canon stand in the way; When the notation is broader than that which is noted, or is neither equal nor equivalent to it, the consequence is valid only negatively: for here it is limited, so that it might not prevail: if the name is derived from that which was formerly and more frequently observed.

XVI. He who rejected the common opinion on the analytical and synthetical Method, and declared there was nothing certain in it, had not yet perceived it correctly: for he was saying that when the Metaphysician deals with first principles, and the Physicist with the first principles of natural things: then they observe not the synthetical but the analytical order. The Politician, however, when he first deals with the city and the republic and afterwards with their parts and species, observes the synthetical Method.

Nec obstat, quod Ecclesia in hac vita obnoxia est ingentibus
aerumnis et deformatur multis scandalis, et adhuc est imbecil-

peccatorum, Filio DEI semetipsum pro ea sanctificante. Iohannis 17. versiculo 19.
Et ipsius sordes reliquas, suo merito tegente, et applicante illi su-

in fidelium cordibus accendente. Hic ornatus, est vestitus ille de-

regis, et gloria, quam internam esse, nec oculis humanis conspici,

roribus, vera Ecclesia iudicio iuxta normam scriptorum Prophe-

of God through the Spirit (Eph. 2, v. 21 & 22); a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people whom God claims for Himself as His own (1 Pet. 2, v. 9). For they not only profess the doctrine of Christianity, but are truly sanctified by the Holy Spirit, as it is said (Rom. 8, v. 14): "For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God." And they retain faith and a good conscience (1 Tim. 1, v. 19).

### XXVII.

These, speaking properly, are the true Church, i.e., the congregation of the members of Christ or the <term>ἁγίων κοινωνία</term> <gloss>communion of saints</gloss>: because they have among themselves the fellowship of the same Gospel or doctrine and of the same Holy Spirit, who renews, sanctifies, and governs their hearts.

### XXVIII.

Whence come those splendid titles, that the Church is called in the Song of Songs <term>καλὴ</term> <gloss>beautiful</gloss> (ch. 1, v. 15), and <term>τελεία</term> <gloss>perfect</gloss> (ch. 4, v. 8), and in which there is no <term>μῶμος</term> <gloss>blemish</gloss> or spot (ch. 4, v. 7). And it is thus commended by Paul (Eph. 5, v. 25): That Christ out of great love gave Himself for it, that He might sanctify it, having cleansed it with the washing of water by the word, that He might present it to Himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing, but that it should be holy and without blemish. Yea, the Son of God Himself pronounces it to be fair (Ps. 45, v. 12), and precious (Isa. 43, v. 4), and holy (Ps. 26, v. 2), and a glorious inheritance (Ps. 16, v. 5).

### XXIX.

Of this kind are those highest eulogies of the holy Church: that it is called the spouse of Christ (Ps. 45, v. 10 & 12; Ezek. 16, v. 8, and often elsewhere); the body of Christ (Rom. 12, v. 5, and 1 Cor. 12, v. 27); the fullness of Christ (Eph. 1, v. 23); the house of the living God, the <term>στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας</term> <gloss>pillar and ground of the truth</gloss> (1 Tim. 3, v. 15); the temple holy to the Lord (Eph. 2, v. 21). Concerning this, it is impious to think or say anything regarding the wicked and hypocrites who remain such.

## Q. III.

### *An Intelligentiis competat numerus Quantitativus?*

Quas ſubſtantias Theologi dicunt Angelos, eas Metaphyſici nominant Intelligentias. Et de his controvertitur hîc : An numerus illis quantitativus tribui poſſit. Pro parte negante viriliter ſtamus, clypeô uſuri tali : Vbi nulla eſt quantitas, ibi nec numerus quantitativus. In intelligentiis nulla eſt quantitas. Ergo. De minore dubitas ? Rectè facis : Nam ſemper dubitare, eſt ſemper in majus verum inquirere. At impugnas eam ? Impugnes, modò non expugnes. Ecquid enim quantititas non ſolis competit rebus materiatis & corporeis ? Negas ? In principia Philoſophica impingis; Contra ipſum Ariſtotelem; contra ipſam veritatem inſurgis. Quantitatis ſpecies inſpicias : Continua eſt, cujus partes communi aliquô terminô copulantur; Diſcretæ contrà partes nullô tali terminô vel conjunguntur, vel coaptantur, Ariſt. l. categ. de quantitate. Vbi v: partes quæſo in Intelligentiis ullæ ? Hæ ſi eſſent, utique ſubſtantiam ipſæ Angelorum facerent vel partibilem vel diviſibilem, utique intelligentiæ ipſæ extenſionem partium haberent, utique corpore conſtarent, utique materiam ſimul cum formâ participarent, quæ omnia abſurda. ### *An quinque sint habitus Intellectuales?*

Quæstio hæc ex 6. Eth. Nicomachiorum desumpta est, ubi Philosopho prolixè satis de habitibus intellectualibus disserit. Notandum verò præ ceteris, habitus eos esse duplices, quosdam instrumentales, qui principalibus tanquam ministri inserviunt, suntque Grammatica, Rhetorica, Poëtica & Logica; quosdam principales, quibus de quæstio præsens est proposita. Furthermore, there is controversy concerning the other limb of the question, and indeed, although we establish that GOD is substance, it is not therefore to be inferred that he is a predicamental substance. We add these reasons. (1) To that to which the definition does not apply, neither does the defined. But the definition of the category of substance does not apply to GOD. Therefore, neither does the defined. Do you want the minor premise proved? Behold! The proof is at hand. For the category of substance is defined everywhere by philosophers as the disposition of genera or species of real, finite, complete, per-se-subsisting Beings that sustain Accidents. But does genus or species have any place in GOD? Is GOD finite? Do accidents fall into GOD? Far be these things, far be they indeed. GOD is some supreme individual and singular above the rest, nor yet such as descends to Universals: GOD is infinite: The attributes of GOD are not accidental, but essential. (2) GOD is a certain Transcendent, and is, if I may so speak, in all genera. For he is the principle of all things, and contains the perfections of all things within himself. Therefore, he cannot be included in one category. Hence the fathers said that GOD is not substance, but above substance. And indeed, if we were to proceed strictly, GOD could not properly be called substance, unless abusively. But that this word is attributed to him happens because we can hardly conceive of him in any other way. Metaphysicians respond briefly thus: Substance is called either from subsisting, because it subsists by itself and not in another, as an Accident; or from standing-under, because it subsists under accidents. Taken in this way, it does not include GOD, but excludes him: Then it signifies only secondary substance, created, finite, and dependent. ### §. 22.

Ex Chirurgia nihil est, quod conducat Hecticis. Aeque enim Venaesectio ac purgatio nocet omnibus ex inanitione morbis, qualis etiam est Hectica, consentiente nobis *Foresto*, qui *liber 4. Observatio* refert, se notasse Matronam Nobilem Hecticam, quae cum per Empiricum Vena ei secta esset, brevi post obiisset. Alterum Hectica detentum, interdictis *Foresti*, suasu Chirurgi & circumforanei, posthabitis, Venaesectionem etiam admisisse, & sequenti die a medicastro Pilula una ex praecipitato sumta, eodem etiam die extinctum esse.

Auri purissimi drachmas duas. fundunt. pulverisant, extrahunt cum Spiritu Salis, abstrahuntque ad Olei consistentiam. quod instillant in Sale Margaritarum pulverisato drachmam unam. ### §. 20.

<margin>Compressed nostrils: thin sharpness of the tip of the nose, hollow eyes: hollow temples: cold skin:</margin>
Besides these, an <term>anamnesis</term> <gloss>recollection</gloss> will also have to be consulted concerning the causes and circumstances preceding the generation of hectic fever, which, the more they are discovered to have had the strength to deplete the inflowing moisture, the less hope they promise for health. Indeed, the signs of the third stage are usually: hollow eyes, dry filth in them, squalor, prominent bones, a vivid luster or the flower of color extinguished, the precordia vehemently contracted, so that they seem to lack intestines. Briefly, the Hippocratic Face, which see described at length in Sennert’s *Praxis*, book on fevers, page 343. Then, the vain administration of things otherwise helpful, and the fact that even the smallest harm of things harmful affects the patient exquisitely, brings not an uncertain suspicion that force has been applied to the innate heat, and that the damage to health has become irreparable. Therefore, the prognosis should be delivered boldly that the <term>marasmodē</term> <gloss>wasting/marasmic</gloss> state of hectic fever is incurable, since there is no help in the nature of things by which this defect, from which hectic fever depends, can be replenished. And so, indeed, if the febrile hectic is simple, it is known by reason of the present state and future event; but when joined with other diseases, it will have to be distinguished from them by their own proper signs.

### §. 21.

There follows now, the nature, difference, and presence of hectic fever being known, its methodical cure. Before we attempt anything to cure the hectic, we will consider circumspectly whether the action of external causes still persists. If so, it must be broken by their swiftest removal. ### XXXIX.

Si quis se interficiat, simpliciterne ad agnatos ibit feudum, an potius causa mortis est attendenda? Quod Zasio probabile videtur.

Redeo ad Definitionem, cujus ultima verba sunt: *quæ vel à solâ bile, vel aliis humoribus simul in majoribus vasis putrescentibus exoritur.* Quibus partim differentia Causi exprimitur: Est enim ratione causæ febris ardens alia à sola bile, quæ subito cum omnium symptomatum vehementia ad statum tendit, & alias *exquisita* seu *legitima* vocatur. Alia à mistis aliis simul humoribus, & *notha* dicitur. Potest autem bilis misceri & simul putrescere cum *pituita*, inde *febris ardens pituitosa* oritur, quæ symptomata habet valdè remissa, tardius ad statum movetur, & quandoque circa vesperam ingravescit: Vel cum *melancholia*, & tunc signa adsunt melancholiæ: Vel cum *sanguine*, uti innuere videtur *Galenus Commentarius 4. XIV. The prediction of the length and brevity of this disease can likewise be sought from <term>Hippocrates</term>. Of those who have burning fevers, he says in <term>Coan Prenotions 1, text 137</term>, "The decision happens on the fourteenth day, either to death or to health." He agrees with this in <term>Aphorism 23, Section 2</term>: *"Acute diseases are terminated by judgment within fourteen days."* Sometimes they do not reach this limit: *"For those whose urine on the fourth day has a reddish cloud, with other signs of a good crisis present, the judgment happens to them on the seventh day,"* according to the same <term>Aphorism 71, Section 4</term>. Likewise, *"if drops of blood with sneezing occur to those beginning to fever, and that which subsides in the urine appears white on the fourth day, they signify that the solution will come on the seventh day"* (<term>Coan 149 and 575</term>). Pertaining to this is <term>Aphorism 51, Section 4</term>, which sounds thus: *"Abscesses in fevers that do not resolve in the first days signify the length of the disease."* In the Greek text is read the word <term>λυόμενα</term> <gloss>resolving/being solved</gloss>, which, as <term>Rolfincius</term> notes in the alleged book, chapter 33, can be taken actively and passively. Actively is better, so the sense is: those abscesses which do not resolve the disease prolong it. Passively, and then the sense is: those to whom abscesses at the ears do not suppurate, <term>αὐτέων ἀπαλλασσομένων</term> <gloss>with them being discharged</gloss>, a relapse occurs, unless they are resolved and vanish in their own way. Compare <term>Coan Prenotions 1, text 138</term>.

XV. Concerning the mode of the outcome, a few things remain to be noted from <term>Galen</term> and <term>Hippocrates</term>. This disease tends toward health by various excretions, as the Coan left written in <term>Coan Prenotions 1, text 150</term>: *"Diseases, precipitous and acute, are finished by judgment when blood flows from the nostrils, and that on the critical day, and when copious sweat has arisen, and the urine is purulent."*

Explanatio textus.
Inscriptio libri de memoria & reminiscentia, materiam eius indicat: vnicu caput duabus partibus absoluitur

Prima pars
Tractat de memoria.
I. Non est idem memorari & reminisci: quia bene memoratiui; ut ingeniosi, no sunt bn reminiscitui.
II. Memoria no est futuri vel presentis, sed preteriti: quia de futuro est spes vel opinio; de presenti sensus: sed de actu preterito memoria: que nec est sensus vel opinio.
III. Memoria est passio alicuius cum factum fuerit tempus.
<margin>Corol. Suppo</margin>
IIII. Sola cognoscentia tempus memorantur.
V. Intellectio no fit sine phantasmate: & ideo intellectus non intelligit sine continuo tempore.
VI. Memoria est passio primi sensitui. probat qa eius est cognoscere tempus; ergo eius est memora: nam sensus cognoscit motu tempus, & magnitudinem: Vnde admittit memoria esse per accidens ipsius intellectus: inquantu recipit fantasma a sensu
VII. Probantur dicta; quia etiam non intelligentia, memorantur vt bruta.
VIII. Non omnia animalia habent memoria.
IX. Licet species rei sit presens: tamen memoria no habet de specie; sed de absente: probat quia si pictura vel sigillu repntat rem preterita, sic species in fantasia: probat hoc primo quia existentes in magno motu non memorant, vt ebrij, infirmi: quia species impediunt. 2. pueri non memorant: quia species impediunt propter fluxibilitatem. 3. Senes non bene memorant; quia ob nimia siccitatem, species non bene recipiunt. 4. quia cito intelligentes, male retinent & memorant.
X. Memoria non est illius speciei: quia tunc esset presentis.
XI. Videtur q memoria sit pntis: quia memoria est ipsius sensus: modo sensus est pntis. 2. quia species in phantasia est, sicut pictura in pariete: modo pictura est psens videnti. 3. Si sensus comunis pot esse absentis; ergo & sensus exterior.
XII. Soluunt predicta; quia licet species vt res quadam sit in re psens: tamen vt est repntatiua alterius sic rei absentis: extendit de modo repraesentans di specierum vt in textu.
XIII. Memoria auget & seruatur per frequentem meditationem: nam anima plus abilitatur, si multotiens memoratur.

Pars secunda de reminiscentia,
XIIII. Reminiscentia no est memoria, nec aliquid de nouo sentire vel intelligere: secundu probatur; quia memoria non fit cum de nouo quid intelligit vel sentit: ergo nec reminiscentia; antecedens patet quia ad memoria requirit interruptio temporis preteriti: & ita memoria supponit prius fuisse actum vel habitu: Sed a memoria differt quia in reminiscentia interuenit obliuio.

XV. Memorari vel reminisci, non est iterato aliquid cognoscere: sed cognoscere hoc le prius sciuissse vidisse.
XVI. Reminiscendi modus fit per hoc q sicut vn motus anime fit post aliu: q ita apprehendat, vnu post aliu: Et ita cu reminisciimur, mouemur de uno actu ad aliu meditando, per simile vel contrariu.
XVII. Cur aliqun reminisciimur facile a longo tempore: & non q heri aut pridie factum? Respondet q hoc est quia reminiscentia fit per alicuius apprehensionem que valet ad apprehendendu.
XVIII. Corol. primum ctro reminisciimur ab illo principio a quo reminiscenda inceperit. Corol. secundu, Bene ordinata facilius reminisciimur q inordinata.
XIX. Cur volens reminisci, non potest aliqun: & dein non qurens, sponte reminisciitur? Respondet quia volens habet multas apprehensiones; que no valent ad illud reminiscendu: & sponte postea venit apprehensio que valet ad apprehendendu.
XX. Volens reminisci cogitet loca in quibus fuit.
XXI. Optimus modus reminiscendi est per diuisionem vt illa septimana fui ibi, diuidendo per dies facile inuenia quid fecerim de vno in alium.
XXII. Cur habentes principiu reminiscendi no reminiscentur? Respondet quia illud principium est indifferens ad multa.
XXIII. Cur aliquando defectuose reminisciimur? Respondetur, q sicut in naturalibus veniunt ita etiam in voluntatis.
XXIIII. Ad reminiscendu confert tempus: ita q cognoscat tempus preteritu esse preteritu: tamen ram memoria q reminiscentia fiunt fine certo tempore: licet res intelligant ad apportionem tpis.
XXV. Contingit errare in reminiscentia & hoc ex parte rei & ex parte temporis.
XXVI. Differt memoria a reminiscentia: quia etsi alia animalia ab homine memorant; sed no reminiscent; cuius ratio est quia reminiscentia fit cu discursu.
XXVII. Reminiscentia est passio corporea: primu signum huius est: quia multi volentes reminisci & non potentes, turbantur: maxime in melancolicis: & est sicut in iratis; qui motus eorum non possunt facile sedare: & propter fortem imaginationem, no cessamus a memoria aliquorum.
XXVIII. Signum secundu est; quia habentes superiora groffa male memorant. Tertium signu quia pueri & senes male memoratiui sunt: pueri ob motum nimiu, senes ob defectum motus.

## Q. Vnica.
### An memoria & reminiscentia differant:
### Articulus. I.

Nota. I. Vt in uerfo ordine curramus istu esse memorandi modum dum videt (gratia exempli) tunc imprimit vna species & similitudo regis in anima, sicut sigillum imprimit formam suam in cera: illa species referuatur in anima: & qui vidit potest de eo cogitare: & tunc dicitur memorari: Hoc supposito scias viam esse memorie acceptionem: nam ipsa potentia memoratiua dicitur memoria: similiter organum reseruatiuum specierum dicitur memoria: & quarto memoria usurpatur pro actu memorandi: & sic loquimur hic de memoria: Et sic duplex est memoria. i. intellectiua & sensitiua. ¶ Et ad memoriam requiruntur sex f. tria representatiua & tria representata secundum Buridanum representata in priori exemplo, sunt rex visus, visio, & tempus preteritum in quo vidit: horum omnium species spectra & similitudines, necesse est, vt habeat anima/si velit memorari.
Nota. II. Iacto illo fundamento, faciliter posse stare differentiam inter memorari, reminisci, & obliuisci: Nam si species fortiter imprimuntur & reseruantur totaliter in anima; vt statim aduertens, tia, statim moueant potentiam, ad iterata rei cognitionem: Et per has species fit memoria: Aut species istae debiliter sunt impresse, aut diuturnitate temporis aut alia causa amisse & corrupte ac totaliter abolite & remote a vi corporatiua specie rum: & tunc dicimur obliuisci: Aut solum sunt remille non penitus perdite/sed confuse & fragiles adhuc modicum haerent in memoratiuo organo/non sufficientes per seipsas mouere potentiam/nisi cum apprehensione alterius, & adiutorio: quo eleuetur & actuetur: & tunc per has species reminisci mur: Accipe symbolum vidisti picturam in pariete: post interuallum redis, vbi pars picture est deleta, & pars manet: iam ex parte picture manentis discursis ad noticiam partis delete: ita contingit in reminiscentia. ¶ Corollarium. Reminiscentia non praesupponit obliuionem totalem/sed partialem: at readdiscentia praesupponit totalem obliuionem. ¶ Corollarium. Sic intelligendus est Auerr. q. res miniscentia fit memoria intercisa. f. obliuioni partiali: est mens Bruxellen. & Ifennach: Addetamen semper quod generaliter memoria extendit se ad reminiscentiam.

Nota. III. Ex his patere diffinitionem memorie datam ab Aristoteles. Memoria est passio vel habitus alicuius cum factum fuerit tempus: est iudiciu de actibus preteritis per modum preteritionis: Non conueniunt hic doctores, cuius potentie fit memoria: Aristoteles concludit eam esse passionem primi sentitui. i. sensus communis: Auicenna. 6. lib. naturali. par. 5. cap. 6. negat memoriam esse in intellectu: G. Ocham q. 12. quarti negat memoriam esse in intellectu: mouetur ex eo/quia ad memoriam requiritur noticia complexa: sed sensus non cognoscit complexive: Item quia memorando reflectatur potentia super actum suum: sed nullus sensus reflectat super actum proprium: plura de his Scot. dist. 45. quarti. q. 3. At bene reluctatur Greg. Arimin. dist. 2. q. 2. art. 2. dub. 3. quia primo memoria est sensus communis sensibilibus: & per accidens seu ex consequenti est in intellectu: tamen intelligibilium memoria primo est in intellectu: Non obstat G. Ocha quia Greg. & Cameracen. q. 3. primi bene ostendunt noticiam sensitiuam esse complexam, de quo in prologo logice. Secundo licet sensus exterior non fit reflexiuus/quia nullus videt se videre: tamen sensus communis bene est reflexiuus super sensus exteriores: quia sentit se videre: Quare duplicem posuimus memoria. sensitiua & intellectiua.

Nota. IIII. ### Articulus II.

**Conclusio.** Memoria & reminiscentia differunt, patet ex dictis & Aristotele in textu. Unde septem colliguntur earum differentiæ. 1. quia memoria fit ratione speciei sufficientis mouere potentiam ad secundam apprehensionem prius cogniti, absque adiutorio alterius speciei: Reminiscentia vero non. 2. Memoria inest etiam brutis, reminiscentia solis hominibus. 3. Memoria quo ad aliquid sequitur memoriam, quo ad aliquid sequitur. 4. Memoria est continuatio referuatio specierum: reminiscentia est quasi earum reuocatio. 5. Memoria est prompta recordatio, reminiscentia non. 6. Reminiscentia præsupponit obliuionem partialem: memoria non. 7. Bene reminiscenti natura liter, frequenter non sunt bene memoratiui.

### Articulus III.

**Problema I.** Cur mulieres subito in non perfecto tempore melius respondent, quia diu deliberant? Respondetur, quia humida habent organa cognitiva & fluida: ideo inconstantes sunt: dum deliberare incipiunt diffluunt de uno medio ad aliud: & ita quanto magis deliberant eo magis confunduntur: quare sunt minus aptæ consilns.

**Problema II.** Cur memorari volentes moueat caput? Respondetur, quia organum memoriæ, particula cerebri, uermiculo simili clauditur, vel aliter opilatur: spiritus in quibus deferuntur species, nec introeunt, nec exeunt/nisi hostiolum tale aperiatur: ideo aliqui mouent vel eleuant caput/dum quærunt oblitum.

**Problema III.** Cur lotio capitis & pedis cum aqua calida conferat memoriæ? Respondet, quia in capite sunt aliquando multi fumi, perturbantes spiritus cognitiuos; qui lotione calidi resoluuntur & euaporant, apertis poris capitis.

<column-break/>

**Problema IIII.** Cur volentes memorari aliquando claudunt oculos? Respondetur, quia motus maiores impediunt motus minores: ne igitur turbentur vel impediantur species memoriatuæ per species visibiles: quia visus est velocissimus sensuum: ideo claudunt oculos.

**Problema V.** Ex quibus attenditur bonitas vel malicia memoriæ? Respondetur secundum Buridanum ex tribus. primo ex complexione organi: quia si fuerit temperata, confert ad memoriam. Secundo, ex apprehensione: quia si fortiter apprehendit cum forti attentione melius id retinet & facilius memoratur. Corollarium: Hinc iuuenes licet natura minus sint memoratiui: tamen de peraccidens aliis quando melius memorantur vel propter nouitatem, vel admirationem/aut quia adeo complacet: ideo fortius imprimunt: & sic memorantur Tertio ex motu vel quiete organi; nam qui in magno motu sunt minus sunt memoratiui, sicut infirmi, irati, formidolosi, pueri & decrepiti.

**Problema VI.** Cur poeta vinum dixerit obliuionem, & Plinius mortem memoriæ? Respondetur, quia vinum est calidum & fortiter euaporatiuum: ideo perturbat suis fumationibus cerebrum, impedit species, debilitat & corrumpit: vt Vergilius eius incommoda describit & Propertius,
Vino forma perit: vino corrumpitur ætas.

### Appendix

De memoria artificiali/cuius inuentor dicitur Symonides & consummator Metrodorus vt meminit Plinius lib. 7. adnotauimus circa textum: ideo nos remittimus ad scriptores de eadem & ad Martinum Ficinum lib. 1. de triplici vita.

It is divided into direct and useful. What the direct one is, the definition provided declares. The useful action is that which, following the example and likeness of the direct one, from a reason of utility, was prepared by the learned in law, whether Roman or modern, for the sake of utility. The Roman learned gave the Confessory action to those who have <term>utile dominium</term> <gloss>beneficial ownership</gloss> in a dominant estate or at least some right in a thing, as are the usufructuary (Law 1, final paragraph, Digest, *On Remissions*), the CREDITOR (Law 16, *On Servitudes*), and the SUPERFICIARY (Law 1, § last, *On Surface Rights*). The moderns wish for it to be competent for other incorporeal things, or rather for vindicating their exercise, such as for jurisdiction, the right of tithes, labor or services, the right of hunting, Patronage, and asserting other rights. 12. But we respond: I. with B. Luther, that this is not to interpret the scriptures, but rather to play with untimely allegories. For Moses recounts history, not allegories.
13. II. That by Light one cannot understand some spiritual, angelic, and invisible light, but rather visible light, is evident from the fact that before the creation of this Light there was darkness upon the face of the abyss, Gen. 1:2. This light was created on the first day so that it might be dispelled.
14. There is also this: before the creation of the Sun and Moon, three natural days preceded it. Therefore, this Light created on the first day must necessarily have been a luminous and visible body, and consequently, not the Angels.
15. Others think they were created on the second day and that some fell immediately, relying chiefly on this small argument: that in the description of that day, Moses did not add, "GOD saw that it was good," etc.
16. Yet in a similar manner, Moses could not have said in the creation of man that they fell immediately, and [yet] "GOD saw everything that He had made, and they were very good," Gen. 1:31.
17. Therefore, since that eulogy of Goodness is repeated twice in the description of the third day, it is more probable that through the carelessness of scribes the sentences were transposed, such that what pertained to the second day was cast over to the third. This was perhaps the reason that the 70 Interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note>, and those who follow them, read that eulogy of Goodness added to the description of the second day.
18. Finally, there are others who think the Angels were created on the third day, with the argument taken from Col. 1:16. For since the Angels are in heaven, and heaven was adorned and completed only on the third day, they could not have been prior to their own dwelling place.

XVI. Therefore, sincere Religion is necessary before all else for a King and a Queen. For just as those who build a house do so from the foundations, so we, who must originate the Republic from its fulcrum and, as it were, its base, must begin with religion. Without it, neither the prince will perform his duty, nor the subjects theirs; without it, society will not exist, because there will be no faith, no justice, no virtue, but fraud, license, impudence, and, in a word, confusion of men and things. Let Religion, therefore, be the bond and firmament of the Republic. J. Lipsius, *Political Monitors*, ch. 1. This religion, however, includes piety and probity. Piety is a right sense concerning God, and the right worship of God known from Scripture; which, to the same Lipsius, is nothing else than the veneration of the recognized Divinity bound by certain laws and ceremonies, *book 1, ch. 3, of Civil Doctrine*.

XVII. Accordingly, let the King, and the Queen who sustains his place, have care not only for the region but also for the religion. The knowledge of secular things ought to be married with unadulterated probity and a not vulgar knowledge of heavenly things; to which the subjects must be habituated in three ways, primarily: 1. by good and religious education, so that immediately from the first times of their age they may duly worship and venerate God, and think correctly about the divine Divinity. 2. by the right institution and sounder doctrine concerning divine worship for those who are older. 3. by the promulgation of laws, by which rewards are proposed for the strenuous worshippers of God and divine things; but punishments are decreed for those who, neglecting God, do what is pleasing to themselves.

Therefore I prefer to refer it to the example of the wind. I understand the heavenly things <term>ἐπουράνια</term> as the question of regeneration <term>τῆς παλιγγενεσίας</term> <gloss>of regeneration</gloss>, which is truly heavenly.

*And no one has ascended into heaven, except he who descended from heaven.*

<margin>By whose benefit regeneration happens to us.</margin> Christ shows by whose benefit regeneration happens to us, certainly not by any merit of our own, but by the work of the Son of God. That it is not by our merit is evident. For no one has ascended into heaven, that is, the righteousness of no one is accepted by God; we are all destitute of the glory of God, all have wandered, there is none who does good, not even one.

We are taught how great is the corruption of our nature, which not even the Angels could compensate for, not to speak of men. These things remove the mask of human merits. Next, they give a reason why men do not grasp heavenly things, because they do not apprehend that Divine light.

But he adds to whom this glory pertains: *Except the Son of Man who is in heaven.* But two propositions are implied: The Son of Man descended from heaven, and the Son of Man is in heaven. The first of these propositions teaches the perfect merit of Christ

### CAP. IV.
#### De
# Nobilitatis Divisione
# Von des Adels Eintheilung.

§. 1. Divisio Nobilitatis non una occurrit. Plato eam in qua-
tuor divisit species, quarum prima est eorum qui claris, bonis
justisque Majoribus nati, Deinde quorum Parentes fuerant nobi-
les ac principes eosdem sic vocabat. Tertio vocari nobiles volebat
quorum majores fama et opinione celebres fuerant, idque vel
ex bellicis rebus clare gestis, vel ex certaminum coronis. Denique
Nobilitatis genus praestantissimum aestimabat, quum quis per se
animi magnitudine excelleret. Confer Plutarchus liber 10. Contra Nobilitatem.

§. 2. Inter Gentis Nobilitatem ac Civitatis cum Privata
distinguit Aristoteles liber I. Rhetorica ad Theodectem caput 5. adeo ut illius
esse splendorem dicat Indigenas ac vetustissimos esse, et primos
duces illustres; multos quoque ex ea gente in rebus, quae expetun-
tur, praeclaros extitisse. Privata vero nobilitas aut a viris aut a
mulieribus est legitimaque ab eis procreatio.

§. 3. Gregorius Nazianzenus triplex facit nobilitatis ge-
nus, unum quod superne originem traxit, ut sunt omnes qui ad
imaginem Dei sunt creati, Alterum, quod a sanguine proficisci-
tur; Tertium a virtute ac vitio agnoscitur. Oratio 18. confer oratio 28.

§. 4. Sex posse Nobilitatis gradus statui Piccolomineus ait;
Primum divinae facit Nobilitatis. (2) Metaphysicae: (3) Inspectricis.
(4) Civilis. (5) Physicae. (6) Fortunae. Quos tamen paulo post
ad quatuor modo formas contrahit, nempe ad Divinam, Mora-
lem, naturae ac fortunae nobilitatem. Divina, ut loquitur Deum
proxime accedit; Moralis quam animi quoque nobilitatem nomi-
nat in compositione morum ac virtutis habitu consistit. Naturae

# CHAPTER III.
-> Of <-
# The Definition of Nobility
-> Concerning the Description of Nobility. <-

§. 1. After tasting the origin, there is now a need to bring forward the definition of various people, so that then the division itself may flow more easily.

§. 2. Moreover, there is one definition among logicians that is nominal, another that is real; the former concerns only the name of nobility; the latter, however, they divide into imperfect and perfect, or said essentially or causally. In this place.

§. 3. *Bodinus* asserts in *book 3 of the Republic, chapter 8, number 350*, that every definition of nobility is imperfect. "It was never possible," are his words, "for a single popular definition of Nobility convenient to all to be brought forward." But who does not see that this is to be understood regarding universal convenience rather than the definition of the essence?

Harum vna Amymone aquam disquirens, telum in ceruum iacit, ac Satyrum dormitantem offendit: Quare ille somno expergefactus puellae ineundae miro desiderio capitur. At Neptuni superuentu Satyrus se dedit in fugam. Amymone autem cum illo concubuit eique Neptunus Lernaeos fontes indicauit. Porro Aegypti filij Argos profecti vt mutuam inter se simultatem compescerent, sese cohortantur, & Danai filias sibi in matrimonium dari obsecrat. In money, however, one does not attend to the physical or material species, but to the formal one or value, unless perhaps something else had been expressly stipulated in the agreement. All who are able to contract can also be obligated by a loan; if they refuse to pay at the appointed time, they can be sued by a personal action for a certain thing. Cited paragraph 1, Institutes on in what ways, etc., unless they are excepted by a special privilege in the law. From a loan, usury generally follows; one type is punitive, another compensatory, another lucrative. Punitive usury is that which is inflicted either by law or by man as a penalty for the delay of those not paying. *Law "Cum quidam," 17, paragraph "Si pupillo," Digest on usury.* This usury cannot be condemned, for it sustains the presumed loss from the creditor's side, which the debtor causes when the debt is not paid by him on the certain day. Compensatory usury is that which is provided so that the just interest that the creditor does not have—because they lack the money—is compensated; it cannot be said that this is forbidden or shameful in general. Lucrative usury is that which immediately makes a profit from a loan, all just title being excluded, and this, by its nature, is shameful and illicit. *Law "Improbum," Code on for what causes someone is infamous.* It is prohibited not only by positive law, Divine (Exodus 23, Luke 6, Ezekiel 18) and Human (entire title of the Decretals of Gregory IX on usury), but also by the law of nature itself.

## XV. Buying and Selling.

Buying is the agreement of a price for merchandise, selling is the opposite: of merchandise for a price. Both, therefore, taken together, are an onerous contract, binding on both sides; namely, the buyer to hand over the price for the merchandise, and the seller to hand over the merchandise for the price. This contract is valid, regularly speaking, before a document is written, *paragraph 1, Institutes on buying and selling*, because it is perfected by the mere consent of the parties. Hence, even before the actual delivery, both the gain and the loss of the sold thing belong to the buyer, *paragraph 5, Institutes on buying and selling*, not to the seller. However, the seller is regularly bound to disclose a defect in the thing they intend to sell, from which grave damage can arise for the buyer, just as they are also bound to guarantee against eviction, *Law "Julianus," 13, Digest on actions of buying*, which includes all interest, damages, and expenses which the buyer has incurred.

Quæso enim edisserant mihi, an significationum diversitas dependeat à solis Consonis an verò à vocalibus? Thus, it is indeed thinner in the abdomen, but toward the diaphragm it is more tumid and ample, so much so that sometimes, if it does not reach the size of the little finger, it nevertheless differs little from it.

Necessity therefore demanding, this duct is now dilated, now rendered narrower again, according to the deficiency or excessive abundance of the humor which it leads from the lower parts to the upper ones.

Nature attributed to this duct very tender valves, resisting the returning humor and impeding the descent of the chyle, which are conspicuous more by the consistency and ligation of the humor than to the eyes. Hence, it was unknown neither to <term>Ruischius</term> nor to <term>Bartholin</term> that, by inserting a fistula, wind cannot be driven downward, nor can chyle by the finger. Therefore, <term>Petrus Vatterius, a Parisian physician and Royal Interpreter of the Arabic language, in his French discourse entitled "Le Cœur Dethrone"</term>, is mistaken and deceives, establishing that not all chyle enters to the subclavian vein because this path is longer, but rather that it occupies the middle place of the mesentery in its receptacle like marrow in the middle of bones, so that it may return into the substance of the mesentery when there is need.

This tube sometimes represents a lymphatic or crystalline color; sometimes, however, it is white, whitening, and most similar to milk, which occurs most of the time. For it changes and varies its color according to the ratio of the contained humor, whether lacteal or lymphatic. For if more copious serum—which, however, rarely happens—passes through those ways, it tints the lacteals not with a white, but with a lymphatic color. For whatever the humor is in the lumbar glands or the <term>receptaculum chyli</term>, such also is seen in the thoracic lacteals, whether white or serous. Thus, the <term>Illustrious Bartholin</term> carefully observed that these changes occur, and that the thoracic ones suddenly swell with the chyle expelled, having been previously contained with serum in the glands.

Especially, however, that this duct varies its color from wine and other more subtle drink, and not so easily into view,

### Conclusion XIII.

Finally, children of brothers or sisters use the right of representation only then if their parents would have been admitted to the succession of the brother. Hence it is clear that if a brother or sister has legitimately renounced the inheritance of a brother, access to it is also precluded for his son. Whether this should be admitted indiscriminately? It is not clear throughout, for if the renouncing brother or sister survived, the renunciation will also harm their children. As Doctors commonly state. But what if the renouncer died before the brother to whose inheritance renunciation was made? Lord Stryck thinks, in *Dissertation on Succession*, dissertation 8, chapter 10, § 83, that the renunciation in this case obstructs the children of brothers, for the reason that this representation differs far from that which obtains in descendants, and the inheritance of collaterals is owed not simply, but only in a qualified sense, and renunciation, regarding the recipient, obtains the force of a last will. We will, however, defend the contrary, for this renunciation has in itself a tacit condition, namely, if it devolves to the renouncer; and an inheritance cannot be renounced unless under the condition if it is deferred. Law *Si ita scriptum* 45, § 1, Digest, *On Legacies 2* <note>original: "ff. de legatis 2"</note>. Zoesius on the title of the Digest, *On Pacts*, number 42.

### Conclusion XIV.

Therefore, if in the aforementioned way no impediment from the person of the parents obstructs the children of brothers or sisters, nor have they themselves renounced the succession, or neglected to accept the inheritance within the prefixed time, this effect results from the right of representation: that they enter the place of their parents in every way, as much regarding advantages as burdens, exercise active and passive actions, and take that portion which their parent would have had if he were alive. The often-cited Novella 118. For in which case representation finds a place, one succeeds not in heads, but in lines <term>stirpes</term> <gloss>branches of a family</gloss>. § *Cum filius* 6, Institutes, *On Heirs Intestate*. For if this is certain, that wherever God is, there also is that man who was assumed by God into the unity of his person. God, however, as no one can deny, is not only in the action of the Supper, but also in the bread and wine of the Supper. It necessarily follows, therefore, that Christ the man, that is, the body and blood of Christ, are in the bread and wine of the Supper. Here someone will object: By this reasoning, the body and blood of Christ will not only be in the bread and wine of the Supper, but also in wood, in stone, in air, in fire, in water, in apples and pears; if someone therefore eats an apple or pear, is he not also eating the body of Christ? Here we must consider that Christ, by his humanity, which is joined with the divine nature in the unity of his person, is present to us in one way in heaven, in another on earth, and in the parts of earthly things, such as in an apple or pear, but in another way in the bread of the Lord’s Supper. For in an apple or pear, he is not there so that he may be distributed to us and taken. But in the bread and wine of the Lord’s Supper, he is so present that he is even there offered to us and taken by us. For neither of the apple nor of the pear did Christ say: Take, eat, this is my body; but he said this of the bread of the Lord’s Supper. Therefore, the body and blood of Christ are distributed in the Lord’s Supper because the bread and wine of this Supper have the word of Christ. In an apple, however, or in cheese, or in beer or water, the body and blood of Christ are not distributed because they do not have such a word of Christ. Therefore, it was rightly said: The word comes to the element (not indeed any element, but to this one divinely instituted) and it becomes a sacrament. §. 2. Moreover, they are called Centenarians (for we not unworthily premise their etymology, so that it may prepare a way for us to the investigation of their genuine and proper meaning) from the <term>Centena</term> <gloss>Hundred, a district unit</gloss>, which was a certain portion and appendage, so to speak, of a certain Territory, District, and County, as the most exquisite Lord <term>Kirchmajerus</term> taught us in the Commentary by which he illustrated the golden booklet of <term>C. Cornelius Tacitus</term> on Germany with great benefit. Just as we politically divide Germany in our time into Circles, as France is divided into Parliaments, Switzerland into Cantons, Silesia into Duchies, Saxony into <term>Weichbildas</term> <gloss>urban/municipal districts</gloss>, Misnia into <term>Ambachtias</term> <gloss>administrative offices/bailiwicks</gloss>, and other regions into other smaller parts and segments, so the Ancient Germans were accustomed to divide their Kingdom into <term>Pagi</term> <gloss>districts/cantons</gloss>, named so from the Greek <term>πηγὴ</term> <gloss>source</gloss> or the Doric dialect <term>παγὰ</term> <gloss>fountain</gloss>, because the portions of the district held together around one and the same river or spring. Yet these were not what they are for us today; rather, they were sufficiently spacious territories, encompassing two or three, sometimes even—as <term>Jod. Willichius</term> testifies in his commentary on <term>Tacitus</term>—twenty thousand men. These districts were not always of the same circumference, but were divided by the Kings into tracts, sometimes wider, sometimes narrower, according to the nature and character of the regions and the multitude of the inhabitants. And even today, traces of these districts, which the ancients called <term>Gow</term> or <term>Gau</term>, as the same <term>Willichius</term> notes, still exist: whence we so often hear the words <term>Nordgau</term>, <term>Zürchau</term>, <term>Rheingau</term>, and others of this kind. The ancients named the districts either from a more prominent river or even from the inhabitants of the districts, which were also called by another name, Counties. For a Count was placed over each district so that he might not only defend the inhabitants of that Diocese or County from the insults of enemies, but also justly judge concerning any causes of the local inhabitants. These districts or Counties, because, as we have seen, they were too ample, containing not only camps, villages, or villas, but even several tracts within their circumference, and could thus not be conveniently ruled by a single Count or District-governor

For if a fornicating woman were denoted here by <term>‘almah</term>, the same would be absurdly repeated, and there would be neither a comparison nor a parable. But for this reason <term>Solomon</term>'s words are called <term>meshali</term> <gloss>proverbs</gloss>, because they claim one thing and intend another. Moreover, it is ridiculous to number the way of a man in obtaining a harlot among the most unknown things, when such disgraces are called "prostitutes" from the open prostitution of the body. And so that the <term>Apellae</term> <gloss>Jews</gloss> may no longer err, we shall show that this passage can be explained otherwise and more rightly. I. If <term>‘almah</term> is taken abstractly, which is not unusual for the Hebrews. Thus the <term>LXX</term> <gloss>Septuagint</gloss> translators: "in youth." As if <term>Solomon</term> were saying that the way of a man in adolescence is uncertain, and so versatile that it can be known with difficulty. But what of the Jews here? <term>Abarbenel</term> writes in his commentary on this place, folio 20, column 2, as follows: "Some of the Christians translate and interpret: 'The way of a man in <term>Alma</term>,' that is, in his adolescence, childhood, and youth. As if <term>Alma</term> had an <term>Aleph</term> at the end, when it nevertheless is <term>He</term>." We are speaking of other things, he of onions. # TO LIVE THROUGH THE YEAR
## COMFORTABLY.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring symmetrical floral and foliate patterns within a square border.</note>
By the reminder of this solemn vow, customarily made around the first Calends of the year when the course of the year is opened, we are invited not unsuitably to consider some of the ancient ceremonies and rites which those who were present observed at the very beginning of the year.

At the beginning, they went to sacrifice to the goddess ANNA PERENNA. Indeed, that this is read without any error in Macrobius (Book 1, Saturnalia, chapter 12) is attested by Barnabas Brissonius (Book 1, p. 58), who cites as witnesses the old Venetian editions and the more recent Gryphian ones, printed by press. On the feast day of this goddess, the common people, scattered here and there through the meadows along the Tiber, lay down with their respective spouses, and prayed that they might be allowed to live through the year comfortably and that each might at the same time receive the years of Nestor and the Sibyl. Ovid notes these rites (Book 3, Fasti) in these verses:

> The Ides are the genial festival of ANNA PERENNA,
> Not far from your banks, O foreign Tiber.
> The people come, and, scattered here and there through the green grass,
> Each drinks and reclines with his peer.

->And a little later:<-

> Yet they grow warm with sun and wine, and they pray for years
> To match the number of cups they drink.
> You will find there one who drinks the years of Nestor,
> And who has become a Sibyl through her own goblets.

The same formula of prayer so pleased Marc-Antoine Muret that he preferred it to all others, when he himself was eagerly striving to pray devoutly—even in public—for a happy New Year's Calends for the Supreme Pontiff himself. For after he had said that the first day of the dawning year had arrived...

The boy was whimpering in the cradle, but *King Herod* was trembling, but all the kingdoms of *those below* were quaking. Go, therefore, all you tapestries of Kingdoms and Halls, and whatever is great on earth and in heaven, only the cradles of this great *Hercules* are great to me! Go, gems plucked from the foreheads of all dragons, from the brains of fish, and from shining shells; nothing is illustrious to us except the illustrious cradle of our *Jesus*, who by his birth prostrated and trampled the *Stygian* and infernal *Leviathan* dragon. Let us beware, however, as we approach this cradle, lest we be found in the count of the impious, who are the seed of the serpent, and lest we imitate the serpents in their vices: for otherwise it is to be feared that we might be torn apart by this *Hercules* in his fury, along with the serpents. The *Serpent*, as Philo’s allegory has it, lacking feet, relies upon its belly; so a man given to pleasures lifts his head with difficulty, weighed down and depressed, with intemperance overturning and supplanting him. Just as the serpent uses clods of earth for food and carries venom in its teeth, with which it is accustomed to kill those it has bitten; so also the minister of pleasures feeds on foods that are by no means celestial, but on those which come from the earth and which the gluttonous appetite of the belly desires immoderately. Let us therefore beware of intemperance, let us moderate our tongue, lest we kill our neighbor with lies and calumnies. Let us proceed to the manger upright, circumspect, and prudent as serpents, while at the same time simple as doves. Then come forward, you too, to this cradle, *Jews*, children of *Abraham* according to the flesh; to you this boy was promised so often, for you he was born, to you he was sent first, whose birth and cradle *Abraham*, your father, longed to see. You await a magnificent *Messiah*, but a pauper was promised; you await a *Leader* fighting in battle, but a *Prince of peace* was promised; you await a *Triumpher*, but he was to be scourged and crucified.
