**The Eighth Matter:** Explaining the meaning of "unbearable hardship." It is not hidden from any knowledgeable person that the intent of the Imams when they say "hardship that is usually unbearable" is that which human custom cannot bear due to the harm it contains, as its examples will follow. This hardship is greater and more severe than the hardship that excuses one from Friday and congregational prayers, such as the hardship of walking in rain and mud; for a person can bear and endure that [latter] hardship without suffering harm, unlike the former. They have mentioned the distinction between the two: if a patient who has an excuse endures a hardship like that of walking in rain or mud and arrives at the time of the Friday prayer, it is forbidden for him to leave unless it becomes excessive, causes harm, and he cannot bear it—which is the "unbearable hardship"—in which case he may leave. It is stated in *Bashr al-Karim*: "Yes, it is recommended for a patient who can bear it, meaning he can bear the hardship that is like the hardship of rain." Sayyid Shattā says in *Iʿanat al-Talibin* on *Fath al-Muʿin*: "And it is established [as valid] for the excused," meaning if he takes the trouble to attend. The end. It says in *al-Iqnaʿ* that the obstacle for someone like a patient is the hardship of attendance, yet he attended while enduring it. The end. These phrases explicitly state that the hardship for which attendance at Friday and congregational prayer is excused—that is, the one like the hardship of walking in rain or mud—is something a person can bear and take the trouble to do, unlike the hardship that permits the multiplication of Friday prayers, for that is the "unbearable" one which a person cannot bear and which causes him harm. Ibn Hajar says in the commentary on

<column-break/>

*al-Mukhtasar*: "It is obligatory for the patient and the like, such as the one excused by rain, if he arrives at the time of its performance, and it is not permissible for him to leave unless there is an unbearable hardship. For example, someone with diarrhea who thought it had stopped, so he attended, then it returned after he had entered the prayer, and he knows within himself that if he stays, his insides will be affected, then he may leave." The end. It states in *al-Tuhfah*: "Unless his harm becomes excessive, such that it increases beyond the hardship of walking in mud to a degree that is usually unbearable, as it appears, then he may leave." The end. By these explicit texts, it is known that the meaning of "unbearable hardship" is that which a person cannot bear and cannot tolerate in any way, but rather suffers severe harm from it. This hardship, with this description, is what is called "unbearable hardship," and it is the one that allows for the multiplication of Friday prayers. It states in *al-Tuhfah*: "The criterion for difficulty is that it contains a hardship that is usually unbearable." The end. Similar is in *al-Nihayah*. As for the hardship that is like the hardship of walking in rain or mud, it does not permit the multiplication of Friday prayers, because a person can usually bear it and is able to tolerate it, so it is not called "unbearable hardship," as has been repeated. It states in *al-Tuhfah*, regarding the excuses for Friday and congregational prayer: "The criterion is that a hardship comes upon him in attending like the hardship of walking in rain or mud." The end. Similar is in *al-Nihayah*. As for the hardship of walking a distance of about a mile or less, as between the two aforementioned mosques, without rain or mud, there is no doubt it is less than the hardship of walking in rain or mud. They have endured it for many years by attending Friday prayer at the old mosque, so it is not an excuse to abandon the Friday prayer, let alone be a permit for its multiplication. By what we have mentioned here, it is known that the claim of the existence of unbearable hardship in walking between the two mosques, as they mentioned in the following question, is false and explicitly so.

умны министры, но Александръ Николаевичъ не довѣряется имъ вполнѣ. на помощь имъ онъ позвалъ знаменитаго доктора Липранди, который лѣчитъ средствами героическими и безъ сомнѣнія скорѣе доведеть до трагедіи. Большое утѣшеніе правительственнаго Петербурга теперь — это народъ и привязанность народа къ царю. Народомъ грозятъ они революціонной молодежи. «Стоитъ только царю махнуть рукою, и студентовъ не будетъ». Да, безъ сомнѣнія не будетъ; да на другой день и дворянства въ цѣлой Россіи не будетъ, а съ дворянствомъ ляжетъ подъ топоромъ все чиновничество; вы сами голубчики пропадете. Ну-ка попробуйте махнуть то рукой! И останутся народъ да царь. Да что станетъ этотъ царь съ этимъ народомъ дѣлать? Вѣдь царь то нашъ бюрократическій, дворянскій, а не земскій. Онъ самъ утонетъ въ дворянской крови, чтобъ уступить мѣсто какому нибудь Пугачову! Не попробовать ли лучше николаевскихъ средствъ: кнута, висѣлицы, да Сибири? Средства хорошія. Но врядъ ли они вамъ нынѣ помогутъ. Вѣдь страхъ убитъ въ Россіи. Нынѣ пойдутъ на лобное мѣсто, смѣясь надъ вами. Да и самымъ трусамъ нѣтъ никакого расчета пятиться передъ вашимъ страхомъ. Въ Россіи есть теперь страхъ, пострашнѣе, — страхъ народнаго воздаянія. А если придется выбирать между топоромъ или висѣлицею, такъ разумѣется, лучше пасть съ сознаніемъ высокаго подвига, чѣмъ жертвою роковаго недоразумѣнія народнаго.

У васъ есть еще одно средство — война. Война національная противъ нѣмцевъ, въ союзѣ съ Италіей и съ Франціей, пожалуй хоть за свободу славянъ, лишь бы только русскому народу не дать свободы. Да, въ самомъ дѣлѣ, идти войною на нѣмцевъ хорошее, а главное, необходимое славянское дѣло, во всякомъ случаѣ лучше, чѣмъ поляковъ душить нѣмцамъ въ угоду. Подняться на освобожденіе славянъ изъ подъ ига турецкаго и нѣмецкаго, будетъ потребностью, необходимостью и святою обязанностью освобожденнаго русскаго народа. Но вы, враги русской и польской свободы, какую дадите вы свободу славянамъ? Или вы хотите повторить въ сотый разъ старый, постыдный обманъ? Не удовлетворивъ никого и не разрѣшивъ ничего у себя дома, на что вы будете опираться? Даже войско придется

Да можетъ быть, вы и расчитываете на ея истощеніе? Можетъ, думаете усмирить ее голодомъ? Смотрите, не ошибтесь въ расчетѣ: война не помѣшала у насъ ни пугачевщинѣ, ни новгородскому бунту.

Но напрасны всѣ наши старанія. Ни война, ни уловки мнимо либеральнаго (?) министерства, ни явная реакція вамъ не помогутъ. Народъ проснулся и ждетъ своего часа, вы сами способствовали его пробужденію. Кокетничая передъ нимъ и возбуждая его противъ молодаго образованнаго поколѣнія, вы сами будите въ немъ сознаніе силы и онъ самъ возьметъ силою то, чего вы ему добровольно дать не хотите.

Для мирнаго исхода настоящаго неотвратимаго кризиса, средство только одно: Земскій всенародный соборъ и на немъ разрѣшеніе земскаго народнаго дѣла. Это средство единоспасительное въ рукахъ царя. Но онъ его употребить не хочетъ. Значитъ онъ хочетъ крови.

Когда правители губятъ страну, частные люди должны приняться за дѣло спасенія. Всѣмъ истиннымъ консерваторамъ, имѣющимъ умъ, чтобъ понимать и предугадывать необходимые происшествія, всѣмъ купцамъ, попамъ и дворянамъ, чиновникамъ военнымъ и гражданскимъ, любящимъ спокойствіе и миръ и желающимъ сохранить жизнь, имущество, женъ, сестеръ и дѣтей, всѣмъ, кому дороги благоденствіе и слава Россіи, я совѣтовалъ бы объ этомъ крѣпко подумать. Вѣдь времени на свободное размышленіе осталось не много. И не худо было бы, еслибъ они, сговорившись, составили между собою громадное консервативное общество, которое я имъ предложилъ бы назвать: «общество для спасенія Россіи отъ близорукости царской и отъ преступнаго министерскаго шарлатанства», и пусть хоромъ подымутъ они голосъ въ пользу Земскаго Собора, какъ единаго средства для предотвращенія кровавой разрушительной катастрофы.

А намъ, революціонерной партіи, что дѣлать? Мы также сплотимся и станемъ подъ знамя «Народнаго дѣла»

To hell with the greatness of Peter, Catherine, and Nicholas, which doomed the Russian people to the shameful role of executioner and at the same time a slave-martyr! We sought power and glory, but found only disgrace; we earned the hatred and curses of the nations tortured by us, and ended in defeat and shameful impotence. Thank God! Our two-hundred-year prison, the Petrine state, is finally collapsing. No force will restore it. We ourselves will push it into the abyss, and freedom to us! Freedom to heroic Poland! Freedom to Belarus, Lithuania, Ukraine. Let everything that wants to be Poland be Poland. Freedom to Finland! Freedom to the Chuds <note>referring to the Estonians/Finno-Ugric peoples</note> and Latvians in the Baltic provinces! And it is time for the Germans to go to Germany.

If the Tsar understood that he must henceforth be not the head of violent centralization, but the head of a free federation of free nations, then, leaning on a dense, reborn force, in alliance with Poland and Ukraine, having torn up all the hateful German alliances, having boldly raised the All-Slavic banner, he would become the savior of the Slavic world!

A dream! I will be told; yes, of course, a dream. But a dream only because there is neither thought, nor heart, nor will in Petersburg, and because our Tsar, unlike King David, always seeks a crown but finds a cow. And let us repeat again: to no other Tsar has so much been given, and from no other will so much be demanded.

There is no hope for Petersburg. The Tsar has chosen a path fatal for himself, fatal for Russia. Like a hopeless invalid, he has surrounded himself with charlatans; the time has come for our Neckers and Calonnes <note>referring to finance ministers of pre-revolutionary France, often blamed for economic mismanagement</note>. The present ministry is <term>jeune, intelligent et fort</term> <gloss>young, intelligent, and strong</gloss>, and imitating the currently friendly government, it wants to dupe Russia with forms without content; with freedom on its tongue, it intends to continue the work of wayward arbitrariness. But they forget only one thing: that deception, possible in a country exhausted by political struggles, is impossible here, because our life only began yesterday, passions are at high tide, not low tide, and our tragedy is still ahead... Мечта! скажутъ мнѣ; да, разумѣется, мечта. И еще повторимъ: ни одному царю не было дано такъ много, и ни съ одного такъ много не спросится.

На Петербургъ надежды нѣтъ. Царь избралъ себѣ путь, гибельный для него, гибельный для Россіи. Какъ безнадежный больной онъ окружилъ себя шарлатанами, — настало время для нашихъ Некеровъ и Калонновъ. Мы хотимъ достигнуть его народнымъ путемъ и не остановимся до тѣхъ поръ, пока оно не исполнится совершенно.

Мы хотимъ и желаемъ:

1. Чтобы вся земля русская была объявлена собственностью цѣлаго народа, такъ чтобъ не было ни одного русскаго, который бы не имѣлъ части въ русской землѣ.

2. Хотимъ самоуправленія народнаго — общиннаго, волостнаго, уѣзднаго, областнаго и наконецъ государственнаго, съ царемъ или безъ царя, все равно и какъ захочетъ народъ. Но чтобъ не было въ Россіи чиновничества и чтобъ централизація бюрократическая замѣнилась вольною областною федераціей.

3. Хотимъ, чтобъ Польшѣ, Литвѣ, Украинѣ, Финнамъ и Латышамъ прибалтійскимъ, а также и Кавказскому краю была возвращена полная свобода и право распорядиться собою и устроиться по своему произволу, безъ всякаго съ нашей стороны вмѣшательства, прямого или косвеннаго.

4. Хотимъ братскаго и, если будетъ возможно, федеральнаго союза съ Польшею, Литвою, Украйною, прибалтійскими жителями и съ народами Закавказскаго края. Готовы и обязаны помогать имъ противъ всякаго насилія и противъ всѣхъ внѣшнихъ враговъ, особливо же противъ нѣмцевъ, когда они сами позовутъ насъ на помощь.

5. Вмѣстѣ съ Польшей, съ Литвой, съ Украйной, мы хотимъ подать руку помощи нашимъ братьямъ Славянамъ, томящимся нынѣ подъ гнетомъ Прусскаго королевства, Австрійской и Турецкой имперій, обязываясь не вложить меча въ ножны, пока хоть одинъ Славянинъ останется въ нѣмецкомъ, въ турецкомъ, или другомъ какомъ рабствѣ.

6. Мы будемъ искать тѣснаго союза съ Италіей, съ которою у насъ чувства, интересы и враги общіе, — съ Мадьярами, ненавидящими, какъ и мы, Австрійскую монархію, если только они совершенно откажутся отъ притѣсненія Славянъ, — съ Румынами и даже съ Греками, когда послѣдніе оставятъ въ покоѣ Булгаръ, и довольствуясь быть собою, забудутъ свои честолюбивыя и свободопротивныя, а главное, суетныя византійскія мечты.

We have mentioned a portion of the discourse on that, even if it does not enter into the chapter of discourse on the species of animals. However, it returns to it from aspects for the reader of this book, from the chapter of discourse on the elephant, the *zandabil* <gloss>a legendary or large animal</gloss>, the monkey, and the swine. And in the bear, the wolf, the hyena, the beast of prey, and the *‘asbar* <gloss>hybrid between a wolf and a hyena</gloss>. Furthermore, wisdom may be more apparent in the fly, despite the delicacy of its form, the insignificance of its value, and the baseness of its condition, than it is in the magnificent horse, even if the horse is more useful in the chapter of Jihad. And in the buffalo, despite the greatness of its form, and in the silkworm and the spider, it is more apparent than in the roaring lion and the murderous eagle. Perhaps mentioning the great of body is more beneficial and more apparent in wisdom than the small, the contemptible, and the few, the trivial, like the tick, the louse egg, the fox, and the louse. The affair of the termite is more wonderful than the affair of the Berbers, and the affair of the crane is more wonderful than the affair of the *‘andabil* <gloss>a small bird</gloss>. For the crane is the greatest of birds, and the *‘andabil* is smaller than a leopard's son. Therefore, Ibn Yunus mentioned some of the slanderers of the narrators, saying, "He strikes between the crane to the *‘andabil*," saying he does not leave a man or a boy but that he slanders him. Similar to this is the satire of Khalaf al-Ahmar on Abu ‘Ubaydah, where he said:

And he strikes the crane to the lark,
Neither an old maid remains, nor a pubescent one.

The "old maid" (*‘anis*) of men is like it of women. We do not prolong the mention of the great of body because of the greatness of its body; we only seek what was more miraculous, more eloquent in wisdom, and more indicative to the common people of the wisdom of the Lord and the favor of this Master. Sometimes the miracle in a thing is only in its form, its workmanship, the structure of its limbs, and the arrangement of its feathers, like the peacock in the curves of its feathers and the varied hues of its colors, or like the giraffe in the wondrous nature of its structure and the positions of its limbs. The discourse on it is similar to the discourse on the *tadarrud* <gloss>pheasant-like bird</gloss> and the ostrich. Sometimes the animal is of wondrous workmanship of body, then it is not remembered after the beauty of creation for a noble character, nor for wondrous knowledge, nor for craft. Among them are those that are like the parrot, the bee, the pigeon, the fox, and the ant. The miracle is not in its depiction, the structure of its limbs, and the arrangement of the colors of its feathers, in the weight of those things we have mentioned. But when children again received the same power from their fathers, being ignorant of troubles, and ignorant of political equality and freedom of speech in general, and having been reared from the beginning in the superiority and greed of their fathers, some rushed toward unjust greed and avarice, others due to drunkenness and the insatiable feasts that accompany these, and others due to the abuse of women and the abduction of children. They changed the aristocracy into an oligarchy. They quickly prepared the same things among the multitudes that were just mentioned. Therefore, it happened that their end was similar in destruction to the misfortunes of the tyrants. For when someone, having observed the envy and hatred existing against them among the citizens, dares to say or do something against those in charge, he finds the multitude completely ready and cooperative. Eventually, they kill them, and they do not dare to set up a king, still fearing the injustice of the predecessors, nor do they dare to entrust public affairs to many, the previous folly still being fresh in their minds. But with the only remaining hope being intact within themselves, they turn to this, and they made the constitution from oligarchic to democratic, and they took the care and trust of public affairs upon themselves. And as long as some of those who had experienced superiority and power are saved, they welcome the present situation and consider equality and freedom of speech to be of the highest value. seed: And the difference in knowledge is according to the difference in the acceptance of the existence of perfection and deficiency. Thus, what is established for existence in the most complete and perfect manner, for knowledge [it is established] in this manner; and what is established for existence in the most deficient manner, [it is established] for knowledge in this manner. The origin of this difference in dominance and subordination of the judgments of necessity and possibility is in the reality that where the judgments of necessity are more dominant, the existence of knowledge is more perfect. And in the reality where the judgments of possibility are more dominant, the existence of knowledge is more deficient. And generally, the specificity of the judgment of the distinction of knowledge from existence, which occurs in the speech of the Shaykh, is in this vein. Otherwise, all perfections after existence, such as truth, power, will, and others, are all the same. And some of them, may God Most High sanctify his secret, have said: "I will present them in the manner of the acting of existing things from the attribute of pervasive knowledge."

Filius ingressus chari vestigia patris,
Impertit patriae commoda multa meae.
Praesidet afflictis, hominesque benignus egenos
Adiuuat, ac miseris ferre paratus opem est.
Ille meis quondam viridantia pascua Musis
Praebuit, & studijs profuit usque meis.
Pro quibus, aeternae coelestia gaudia vitae
Omnipotens illi des aliquando Deus.
Haec exempla tuae solers imitabere gentis,
Exprime maiores inclyte sponse tuos.
Sic tua laus crescet, tua sic generatio fiet
Clarior, & tua sic fama perennis erit.
Sed quoniam per te sapientius ista reuoluis:
Admonitu cessent carmina nostra suo.
Sicut equus fortis forti de semine natus
Non metuit strepitus, moesta nec arma fugit.
Haud aliter sequeris clarorum facta parentum,
Nec sinis ingenium degenerare tuum.
Magna tuam merito sustentant gaudia mentem
Sponsa, quod in thalamos vir venit ille tuos.
Non ego, si Pylium dicendo Nestora vincam:
Eloquio maior si Cicerone forem:
Omnia pro merito, quae tanti gloria sponsi
Postulat afferri, commemorare queam.
Quin igitur potius iuuenem mea Musa maritum
Deseris, & castae virginis ora petis.

Foeminei salue decus inclyta nympha pudoris,
Salue virginei gloria magna chori.
Prosperet ipse tui sanctissima iura cubilis:
Qui primus thalami fautor et autor erat.
Qui primus reperit dulcis connubia taedae,
Quicque tori sacras fertur amare faces.
Ille tui placidè fortunet foedera lecti
Euphrosyne, tanto digna puella viro.
Rara tibi facies est, et praestantia formae
Tanta tuae reliquas te superare facit.
Caeruleos oculos sublimes tollis in auras
Saepius, et rutilo tota colore nites.
Qualis ab oppositi splendenti lumine Solis
Crebrius infectis nubibus esse solet.
Siue pruinosae matri, quae sydera caeli
Pellit, et Eoâ ducit ab axe diem.
Talis in ore color spectatur, vix mihi tantum
Lilia purpureo sanguine tincta rubent.
Formosum decorat diuina modestia vultum:
Mitis es, ac omni rusticitate cares.
Flauicomos ceruix demittit eburnea crines
Expoliuntque tuas florida serta comas.
Brachia sunt niueis tibi candidiora ligustris:
Ornatum referunt singula membra suum.
Tu quoque sis hilaris, sis toto pectore laetus
Sponse, quod amplexus expetit illa tuos.

Moreover, he knows how to settle doubtful lawsuits,
And to reconcile fierce enemies with enemies.
Often someone, held by an ambiguous case,
Nurtures the wars of judgment for a long time.
To him he has learned to set forth the strengths of his own cause,
And to recite the legitimate law of his own matter.
I pass over the exceptional love of holy piety,
And with what diligence he cultivates virtue.
And with what zeal he reveres God, and amplifies
His honor, the slender Muse cannot report.
But those gifts wish to be spoken of in a weightier song,
Such as Virgil uses to sing of bloody wars.
Great joys deservedly sustain your mind,
Bride, because that man comes into your chambers.
But if you marvel more at the lineage of an ancient family,
And the honor of the highest nobility captivates you.
He is also born of distinguished parents by ancestry:
And he shows famous ancestors in a long line.
Whom, so that I do not bring weariness to those reading a long song,
I do not wish to recount all in this place.
Let it suffice to celebrate a few of their praises
With a sincere heart in a slender style.
How many advantages your grandfather gave to Memmingen,
When he had held the office of Consul:
It is known, and the walls of the grateful city testify to this,
Which rejoice to have produced such a man.

tem widerkommen: Wir mögen gleichfalls von dem Urdorffer Bad / und selbiger ganzen Gegend mit Wahrheit sagen / sie seye ein Samler viler Lustbarkeiten / und also beschaffen / daß dieselbigen nicht nur den Leib / sondern auch Geist und Gemüth zu erquicken nichts ermanglet. Welches wir dem günstigen Leser lieber auß dem Augenschein und Gebrauch des Bads wöllen erfahren lassen / als ihne mit längerer historischer erzehlung ferner aufzuhalten.

Ist kein Graß noch Kraut so klein / daß nicht preißt den Schöpffer seins / so sagt uns schlüßlich die natürliche Vernunfft / wie hoch wir der wundersamen Güte GOttes um dieses und vil dergleichen Heil-Wasser in unserm Zürich-Gebiet zudancken haben / den besten danck aber werden wir ihm geben / wann wir sie nicht nur unter die Natur-Wunder und Gaaben GOttes werden zellen / sondern auch GOtt zu Ehren brauchen / und den Gebrauch derselben durch keinen unmäßigen / übermühtigen / wühlenden und undanckbarn Mißbrauch beflecken;

**Ehrenvester** / Hochgelehrter Herr Schwager Doctor Ziegler/ etc.
Weilen ich vernomen / daß die dritte Beschreibung des Bads zu Urdorff solle in den Druck verfertiget werden / wil Ich auch mittheilen was in wehrender Zeit meines 15. jährigen Pfarr-Diensts zu Urdorff / von mir beobachtet worden. Dieses berühmte Bad ist herzlich gut in dem <term>Calculo</term>, dann es erweichet / und treibt auß den Nieren- und Blasen-Stein / Sand und Grieß / wie neben mir solches noch vil Ehrliche Personen in der That erfahren: <term>Cholericis</term>, Gall- oder Gelbsüchtigen / ist es auch fürtrefflich bequem / von welchen es ein Wust (f. b.) außgeführt / davon die Zeugen meistentheils diser zeit noch im Leben sind. <term>Febricitanten</term>, (was gattung es seyn mögen) war es dienlich: Vil Außgedörte / Schwein- und Lungensüchtige sind wägen schwachheit in sänften dahin gebracht worden / die nach vollendung der Cur frisch und gesund zu pferd heimreiten können. Dem verderbten / undäuigen magen bringt es widerum treffenlichen appetit und macht Lust zum essen. <term>Acuire</term> und schärfft höchstverwunderlich die Augen / also daß vil Personen / welche vor der Baden-Cur Gläser oder Brillen gebrauchen müssen / hernach ohne dieselben schreiben / lesen und andere Geschäft verrichten können. Weiß mich auch wol zu erinnern ansehnlicher Ehrenleuten / die es wegen Unfruchtbarkeit besucht / und hernach die <term>efficaciam</term> und erfreuliche Würckung treffenlich gerühmt haben. Disem segen Gottes / mein Nachfahr / H. Pfarrer Wirtz auch Zeugnuß gibt. Kostlich an dem ort ist zu dem Bad ein dienstbarer / holdseliger / freundlicher / liebreicher Wirth und Gastgäb / wo der Fehler an dem Ort / ist alle Anmuhtung verlohren.

<header>Of the precious bath at Urdorff.</header>

<margin>Situation</margin>
Regarding the well-situated and delightful location of the Urdorff bath, where nature plays all around the entire village and delights the eyes with its varied features, with surrounding mountains, lovely valleys, grass-rich meadows, wide fields, shady forests, adjacent parish churches and villages, convenient paths towards the Limmat river, and across a pleasant height into the trout- and crayfish-rich Reppisch valley; likewise, regarding the convenience of obtaining all necessary food supplies not only from the city of Zurich and from Bremgarten, but also from neighboring towns according to every wish, there is no need to use more words or fill many pages.

Just as the entire Swiss Confederation is completely enclosed toward the sunrise and noon by a high, mountain-like living green hedge, but toward the midnight [north] and evening [west] is separated from Germany by Lake Constance and the Rhine river, and is to that extent bordered; so too does this Urdorff bath have its situation, mountain and valley, forests and fields, water and meadows, such that one bath-guest can find his amusement in one thing, and another in something else.

<margin>(a) Method. leg. Histor. Helv. p. 242 243. (b) Athanas. Kirch. Mund. sub-terr. (c) Glar. descript. Helvet. p. 28. & panegyr. p. 33. (d) Schvuyzer. descr. Helv. p. 6.</margin>
Regarding the entire Swiss Confederation, it is judged by several scholars to be the highest land in Europe, likewise that it is as much as the *Cor Europæ* <gloss>Heart of Europe</gloss>, as a land that borders Germany, Italy, and France, and lies between them to separate them; as a land filled with the highest and therefore very fertile and productive mountains; as a land that carries under these mountains the most noble minerals, and from the *Mineralibus* <gloss>minerals</gloss> also come the healthiest and most powerful waters, of which the late Herr Doctor <term>Hottinger</term> thought with no small surprise and with some further specification (a); yes, as a land into which no rivers flow from other countries, but on the contrary, because of its height, quite a few flow from it to other neighboring countries; so that both the world-famous German Jesuit (b) *Athanasius Kircherus* in his subterranean world-contemplation, and the famous Swiss writer *Henricus Glareanus* in his writings, hold the Swiss Confederation to be a wonderful collector of water. *Kircherus* shows a water-holder or subterranean fountain-chamber under the *St. Gotthard* mountain, of the opinion that the Rhine, the Rhone, the Inn, the Linth, the Aare, the Reuss, and other rivers originally come from it. (c) *Glareanus* counts 24 navigable lakes, six strong-flowing ship-bearing rivers, together with a considerable number of cold and warm wonder-springs and wonder-fountains on high mountains, under cruel rocks, in deep ravines, which partly have their regular course, partly disappear for certain months, and afterwards for certain summer months to the benefit of humans and cattle

A truth-telling oracle; but you, whose fates follow,
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*

Who may flood your mind with heart-bending love,
And prepare to join you in languid sleep,
Laying her smooth arms under your robust neck.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
No house has ever woven such loves,

Who very often, a victor in the wandering contest of the race,

# TH. XI.

## Octavò differt gravitas vitiorum secundum Dignitatem virtutum, quibus opponuntur.

<margin>3. 2. q. 73. art. 4.</margin>
*Quod ex Aristotele Thomas probat: Dicit Philosophus, quod pessimum optimo contrarium est. Optimum autem in moralibus est maxima virtus: pessimum autem gravissimum peccatum.* Quandoquidem verò de mutua virtutum inter se comparatione, quaequae Principem in illis locum obtineat, nondum expedita lis est, neque de vitiis hoc respectu determinare quicquam, integrum erit. Fulgent profectò quasi stellae virtutes omnes, earumque radiis noster hic tenebrarum orbis redditur illustris. quae tamen earum magis fulgeat, solisque instar ad caeteras se habeat, non facilè esse judicare, fatetur *Piccolomineus*. 

<margin>Phil de Mor. Gr. 4. c. 47. & 49.</margin>
Et pro singulis quidem hic ipse aliquid affert, cujus intuitu principatum satis sibi probabiliter vendicent, quod & rationibus, & assensu sapientum confirmat; monetque inprimis, pro diversa hominum conditione judicia de hac praerogativa multum variare, praeferentibus, qui in Magistratu constituti sunt, justitiam, Ducibus exercituum atque militibus, fortitudinem, viris splendidè natis & educatis magnificentiam, &c. his tamen non obstantibus, figi sententiam de praelatione absolutè in una aliqua posse reputamus. quod malumus exprimere verbis celeberrimi moralium Doctotis in Italia jam laudati, quam nostris: 

<margin>Phil Mor. Gr. 4. c. 51.</margin>
> *Quia ea virtus absolutè optima censeri debet, cui optima praestantiae ratio, ratio dignitatis praestantissima à fine praesertim petenda est: finis virtutis est actio, actionum praestantissimae illae sunt, quae ex iustitia prodeunt: jure igitur iustitia principatum obtinet. Quod justitiae actio optima sit, constat: nam munus eius est actiones nostras erga alios componere, caeteros congruenter gubernare, dissipatos homines congregare, congregatos servare, Respublicas, hominumque cum parvos, tum magnos coetus aureis ligamentis perstringere, prodesse omnibus, & obesse nemini, quod virtutis summopere est proprium.*

These later words provide us with the opportunity for inquiring how harm, according to being intended or foreseen, increases the gravity of sin in various ways.
<margin>Qu. cit. art. 73. <gloss>Question cited, article 73</gloss></margin>
But due to the narrowness of the pages, we refer the matter to <term>Thomas</term>, who considers harm first as foreseen and intended, then as foreseen but not intended, and finally as neither foreseen nor intended, and hence pronounces on the aggravation of the offense. That doubt, however, which is moved by the same man, must not be passed over. Namely, when someone induces a woman to commit fornication, he induces her into a mortal sin, and so, as far as in him lies, deprives her of the life of grace; but a murderer deprives another of life only naturally, which is less harm than the former: and yet murder is held to be a worse offense and is punished more severely than simple fornication. Answer: The gravity of murder prevails because the murderer directly intends the harm of his neighbor; but the fornicator, who provokes a woman, does not directly intend her harm, but pleasure. Secondly, the murderer is by himself a sufficient cause of bodily death, in such a way that the other contributes nothing: but he who acts by persuasions leaves something to the will of the other, so that he is not the unique and sufficient cause of that spiritual death which follows. The matter is different in violent rape, which is therefore compared with murder (Deut. 22:26), so that we say nothing of the means of restitution, which remains here but is lacking there.

### TH. X.
### Seventhly, perversity takes increase from circumstances.

Sometimes when one is not acting rightly, sometimes when several are not. For although the righteousness of all circumstances is necessary for good acts, for this purpose, however, that someone might depart from the order of reason, even the neglect of one due circumstance suffices, which they express by the common saying of <term>Dionysius</term>: "Any single defect causes evil, yet good is caused by an integral cause." But the difference to be noted here is between the circumstances themselves, some of which transfer the moral act into a new genus of malice: others leave it in the same genus, but nevertheless increase the reason for the sin. Thus, the example of fornication, which <term>Aquinas</term> brings into the medium, consists in this: that a man approaches one who is not his own; but if this circumstance is added, that he vents his lust on the spouse of another, it is transferred now into another genus of sin, namely injustice, in as much as a man usurps the thing of another. Whence adultery is called a graver offense than fornication. Let the example of the latter be some angry person, who gets angry when he ought not, and at whom he ought not, and with an inconvenient gesture, which triplet of circumstances certainly makes this anger graver than if at least one of them were violated. Just as a sickness is graver which infects more parts of the body. It happens, however, sometimes, that some circumstance does not add a new deformity, but only increases that which had come from elsewhere. Just as taking another's property constitutes theft: but if this is added, that he takes much of another's property, it will be a graver sin. Nor is there any reason for someone to say that a circumstance, if it is evil, constitutes a certain species of sin by itself. For this is false, or at least not universal, since it can add a reason for malice within the same species. About which see <term>Thomas</term>. We add at least this, since it can also be referred to among circumstances, how often, or properly—which <term>Cajetan</term> denies—or by analogy, that also in the weighing of an offense is not to be passed over. Whence <term>Grotius</term>: "A greater depravity also appears if someone has sinned more often: because habits are worse through evil acts."

### XLIV.

Judæi insuper, ad servandum eundem in mensibus singulis tempestatum tenorem, mensem integrum adjiciunt, qvoties Epactarum numerus dies triginta superat.

### XLV.

Sunt autem Epactæ dies undecim, inter Solarem annum 365. & Lunarem 354. dierum, differentiales. Qvas subinde oportet crescere, si annos ejusmodi plures ab uno qvodam communique principio, sine compensatione, fluere permittamus.

### XLVI.

Atque sic enascitur ille Lunaris, qvem antea Embolimæum dixi. Qvi cum ex motibus Lunæ ita temperatus sit, ut menses annorum communium etiam, qvâ fruitionem perpetuarum tempestatum, ejus beneficio, ad leges revolutionum solarium qvodammodo restituantur; tota forma talium annorum composita meritò censetur, annique ipsi nec merè Lunares, neque solares etiam, sed Lunæ-Solares habendi sunt.

### XLVII.

Anni denique Civiles alii aliis liberiores sunt. Olympiadici modò 360. modò 361. vel 362. itemque alii 390. 391. 392. diebus absolvuntur. Nabonassarei, sive Ægyptii qvidem 365. dies habent, ut annus Julianus Communis: sed sine omni intercalatione.

### XLVIII.

Itaque vaga admodum est ista annorum ratio, si cum forma Juliana comparetur. Neque enim ibi certum perpetuumque initium invenit annus Ægyptius, sed elapso qvolibet qvadriennio, die integro à Julianis differt, propter diem intercalarem, qvem qvartus quisque Julianus recipit, ille verò non admittit.

### XLIX.

Hinc caput ejus omnes menses anni Juliani regrediendo percurrit, donec absolutis Julianis 1460, compleantur Ægyptii 1461. Tunc enim ambo ad unum communeque principium recurrunt.

that is either Physical, and refers to one of the fixed stars: or hypothetical, and refers to a cardinal point of the Ecliptic, whether the Equinox or the solstice. If the former, it is called the sidereal Solar year. If the latter, it is called the Tropical, or Returning, Solar year.

### XXXVIII.

The Tropical Year, according to the calculations of Danish astronomy <note>refers to the work of Tycho Brahe</note>, consists of three hundred sixty-five days, five hours, 48 minutes, and 55 seconds. The sidereal year exceeds this by an interval that, on the part of the Sun, corresponds to the motion of the fixed stars in the order of the signs. Since this is 20 minutes and 18 seconds and 20 thirds, it is necessary that the sidereal year be completed in 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, 13 seconds, and 20 thirds.

### XXXIX.

The Lunar year is composed of several lunations, or synodic revolutions of the Moon to the Sun. It contains twelve, whenever it is a Common [year]: but thirteen, when it is <term>Embolimæus</term> <gloss>intercalary/leap year</gloss>. The former therefore contains 354 days, 8 hours, and 49 minutes. The latter contains nearly 383 days, 21 hours, and 33 minutes.

### XL.

Furthermore, the additions of hours and minutes are neglected in civil use: yet in such a way that, once they have been omitted time and again, they are compensated for at an appropriate time by intercalation.

### XLI.

Let the Julian year serve as our example: although it consists of 365 days and six hours, it is believed to have completed its orbit when just as many days have passed. But so that no account is taken of those hours, every fourth revolution, when it is necessary for that deficit to grow into twenty-four hours, the year is increased by an entire day, and from a Common [year] it becomes a Leap year of 366 days.

### XLII.

Yet our year is not accurately solar, but exceeds it by about eleven minutes. This is the cause of the anticipation of the equinoxes and solstices in the Calendar.

### XLIII.

In the Lunar year, adapted for civil uses, compensation is soon carried out by alternating months, hollow and full: of which the former are completed in twenty-nine days, the latter in thirty days.

Cæterùm horarum ac scrupulorum appendices in usu civi-

### XLI.

Sit nobis exemplo annus Julianus: qvi tametsi 365. diebus

### XLII.

Neqve tamen accuratè solaris est annus noster, sed eum un-

qvinoctiorum & solstitiorum in Kalendario.

### XLIII.

In anno Lunari, ad civiles usus accommodato, mox alter-
nis mensibus, cavis & plenis, peragitur compensatio: qvorum

What shall I prefer to what? Shall I follow? And shall I defile my hands
With the blood of my son, unhappily? Ardor forbids: and the force
Innate in my deep mind: sorrow prohibits: Therefore, conquered by sorrow,
Shall I ignore the commands of the supreme parent?
Not so. But rather let these bonds of love cease:
Let nature changed unlearn its laws:
And let that fatherly sorrow flee far from my mind.
I will follow you: and I will follow your orders, O greatest King of heaven;
Thus it is fixed: nor will the judgment once fixed yield;
Only you, you provide strength and robustness to my mind,
Highest GOD: and be present, and strengthen the Divinities.
    Thus he relates, and turning his eyes to the stars of heaven,
He sees the dawn bringing itself in saffron chariots
Through the air and the clouds far away: preceded by Lucifer,
Who is most illustrious on his white horse, and with his curved horn
Manages the journey: and gathers all the stars here and there:
And now drives the nights, now sated, to the waves of Tethys <note>the sea</note>.
And there is no delay: he makes vows to the gods above: and with his vows completed,
He snatches his body from the bed: and awakens his servants and his household:
Then he calls his son, but not, as before, with a fatherly
Voice. Suddenly, having left his sleep and bed,
The son is present: and he seeks his father: and he tires out the servants.
Quickly they obey him, eager, and do all things.
And now they prepare themselves for the journey: now they lead the usual
Beast of burden from the high mangers with goads.
Now they again split the wood with a strong axe,
And with these they load the ribs of the slowly walking ass.

14. The concept of an actual nature does not belong to Matter in itself, but only insofar as it underlies a form.
15. Substances, both through themselves and through their accidents, exert an immediate and true influence upon an effect, whether substantial or accidental, provided they are rightly applied.
16. Quantity has no parts in act; or rather, it contains indivisibles that are real indeed, but distinct only formally.
17. Motion is given per se only to three predicaments, namely, to quantity, quality, and where <note>the category of place</note>.
18. If a man existing in Ingolstadt were replicated in Rome and died there, he would also have to die in Ingolstadt.
19. Permanent things, speaking per se, do not have a certain mode of beginning or ending, but can vary in their beginning and ending according to the variety of intervening causes and conditions.
20. Even if a simple body does not imply it, the Heavens are not of this kind, but consist of matter and form.
21. In conversion, the term from which must absolutely cease so that it no longer exists in the nature of things.
22. The growth of living things is essentially distinguished from the growth of non-living things: yet it does not really differ from nutrition, even if action is conceded to be a mode.
23. It is not repugnant to nature that there be some mixture equal in weight according to active qualities, although equality in weight according to motive qualities seems impossible.
24. The rational soul, even if it demands to be created connaturalistically, as a spiritual form, can nevertheless be generated through an obediential power.
25. The soul informs no fluid parts, such as blood,

<column-break/>

semen, fat, and so forth. It does, however, inform solids such as hair, feathers, and beaks.
26. The integral parts of a material and divisible soul are not heterogeneous but homogeneous.
27. The state of separation for the Soul itself is neither natural nor properly violent, but is preternatural.

### FROM METAPHYSICS.

28. Being is analogous with respect to God and creature, substance and accident, and so forth.
29. A possible creature, before it is produced, has no actual being, and thus a stone, for example, not existing, is said to be possible here and now, because those predicates which are apprehended in the stone are not productive of a contradiction.
30. To constitute different predicaments, a real distinction between them is not required, but one of reasoned logic suffices.
31. Substance is that which is intended for its own sake, not on account of another thing adequately distinct from it: whence an accident is that which is intended by nature on account of another thing, from which it is adequately distinguished.
32. Predicamental relations of the third kind are not mutual; whence no relation looks to a term as relative, but as absolute.
33. There are transcendental relations, distinct from predicamental ones in this: that the latter look to another purely as a term, while the former do not.
34. That God exists can be demonstrated naturally only *a posteriori* <gloss>from effects to causes</gloss>.
35. Angels can naturally move themselves with motion both continuous and discrete, so that they arrive from one place to another without passing through the intervening space.
36. A being of reason can be produced by the created intellect alone.

སྒོམ་མེད་ཡིན་ཀྱང་། །སྒོམ་མཁན་རིག་པའི་ངོ་བོ། །ཁྱབ་རྡལ་ཆེན་པོར་ཞོག་ཅིག །གཉུག་མ་སེམས་གྱི་གནས་ལུགས། །གདོད་ནས། སྤྱོད་མེད་ཡིན་ཀྱང་། །སྤྱོད་དང་
བླང་དོར་གཉིས་མེད། །མ་བཅོས་ལྷུག་པར་ཞོག་ཅིག །གཉུག་མའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་གནས་ལུགས། གདོད་ནས་ལྷུན་གྲུབ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་། །འབྲས་བུ་སྒྲུབ་བྱའི་ཞེ་འདོད། །
སྤྲོས་བྲལ་དང་དུ་ཞོག་ཅིག །དེ་ལྟར་སྐྱངས་པའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར། །གནས་ལུགས་བརྟན་པ་ཐོབ་ན། །ཉོན་མོངས་འཁྲུལ་པ་དག་ནས། །སངས་རྒྱས་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པོ། །
ཅེས་གསུངས་སོ།། །།ཡང་གནས་མཁན་ཆེན་ཉི་མ་གྲགས་པ་ལ་ཀ་སྨད་སུམ་ཅུ་ལ་དྲངས་པ་འདི་གསོ། །ཀ་སྐྱེ་མེད་ཀྱི་དགོངས་པ་རང་བྱུང་བ། །ཁ་མཁའ་ལྟར་
དངས་པའི་ངང་ཉིད་ལས། །གང་དགག་སྒྲུབ་མེད་པའི་རིག་པ་དེ། །ང་དངོས་མེད་པ་ཤིས་ཀྱི་ངང་། །ཅ་བཅོས་མ་མེད་པའི་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱིས། །ཆ་ཆོས་སྐུའི་བྲུས་མ་ཐོབ་བར། །ཇ་ཇོ་བཟངས་བྱེད་ཀྱི་

དོན་སྒྲུབས། །ཀ་སྨད་སུམ་ཅུའི་ཉམས་དབྱངས་འདི། །སེམས་ལ་ཤར་ནས་བྲིས་པ་ཡིན། །ཅེས་གསུངས་སོ།། །།ཡང་ཕག་ལོ་ལ་
ལྷ་ལུང་དུ་ནང་སོ་བསོད་ནམས་རྒྱལ་པོ་སྐུ་གཤེགས་པའི་དུས་སུ། ནང་སོ་ཚོས་མཛད་ཡུམ་སྲས་ཀྱིས། སྐུ་གཤེགས་ཀྱི་ཡར་འདྲེན་ལ་ཕེབས་དགོས་ཞུ་བ་བྱུང་
ཀྱང་། དེ་དུས་ཐུགས་མ་སྐབས་པར། ཚེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རིང་སྲེལ་གཅིག་དང་བཅས་ནས། ནང་སོ་ཆོས་མཛད་ཡུམ་སྲས་ལ་སེམས་བསོ་བ་སླབ་བྱའི་རིམ་
པ་འདི་ཡི་གེར་བྲིས་ནས་གནང་ངོ་།། །།སྐྱབས་གནས་བློ་གཏད་ཐུབ་པའི། །དཀོན་མཆོག་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་ལ། །ཕྱག་འཚལ་སྐྱབས་སུ་འཆིའོ། །
སྔོན་ནས་ལས་འབྲེལ་ཟབ་པའི། །དཔོན་པོ་ཡུམ་སྲས་བསན་དང་། །ས་སྟེང་གནམ་འོག་ཕྱོགས་མཚམས། །མཐའ་དབུས་གང་དུ་ལྟས་ཀྱང་། །

བཞིན། །རིམས་ཀྱི་རིམས་ཀྱི་ལངས་ནས། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཟང་མཐའ་མེད་དོ། །མི་ལུས་རིན་ཆེན་སྙེད་དུས། །བྱ་བ་ཀུན་རྣམས་ཐོང་ལ། །འབད་པ་ཆོས་
ལ་བགྱིས་དང་། །གཏན་གྱི་མདུན་མ་ཡིན་གྱིས། །གནས་སྐབས་དེ་ཆེའི་བྱ་བ། །ཐམས་ཅད་སྒྱུ་མའི་ཆོས་ཅན། །ཅི་བྱས་ཕན་བ་མེད་ཀྱིས། །མི་རྟག་རྒྱུད་
ལ་བསོམས་ཤིག། །ཚེ་འདིའི་བྱ་བ་བོར་ལས། །བརྟན་གྱི་མདུན་མ་བསྒྲུབས་དང་། །དོན་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་ན་ད་རེས། །ཕྱི་མ་ཅི་འགྱུར་ཆ་མེད། །རང་དབང་ཡོད་པའི་
དུས་འདིར། །རྣམས་གཡེངས་བྱ་བ་སྤོངས་ལས། །རང་བྱུང་རྫོགས་པ་ཆེན་པོའི། །གདམས་པ་ཟབ་མོ་འདི་ལ། །ཉམས་ལེན་འབད་པ་བགྱིས་ཤིག། །འདིར་
བདེ་ཕྱི་མ་སྐྱིད་དོ། །ད་ལྟའི་རྒྱལ་སྲིད་འདི་ཡང་། །བྱམས་སེམས་ཆོས་ཀྱིས་སྐྱོངས་མདོས། །སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་ལ་ཕན་ན། །བདེ་བ་རང་ལ་ཡོང་གིས། །སྦྲང་་་བན་
པད་གླིང་སླབ་བྱ། །སེམས་ཀྱི་་་དཀྱིལ་དུ་འཆོངས་ཤིག། །ང་ཡང་ཕག་ཟླ་ཙམ་ལ། །ཡོད་་་གིས་དེ་དུས་ཡོན་མཆོད། །བཀའ་སྒྲོས་ཞིབ་པར་བྱའོ། །

གདུང་བསོབ། རིག་འཛིན་ཆེན་པོ་མེ་ཏོག་བསོད་སྙོམས་མཛད་པའ་ཆེ། དགོན་པ་པད་མ་གླིང་གི་ལྷོ་ནུབ་ཀྱི་འཚམས། ཡུལ་ཉམས་དགའ་བི་ཞེས་བྱ་བར

སྤྲོས་པའི་དྲན་པ་ལུ་གུ་རྒྱུད། །ཡུལ་དྲུག་ས་གཞི་སྒྱུ་མའི་གཟུགས་སྟོན་ཅིང། །བདེན་མེད་འདི་ཡིས་བདེ་བའི་ལམ་གཏོར་བ། །ཆུ་ཟླའི་མིག་སྒྱུ་ལྟ་བུའི་
ཁམས་པ་གཟིགས་ལགས་སམ། །ཅེས་གསུངས་པ་དང། ཡང་ཞུས་་་པ། དང་བ་འགྱུར་མེད་བརྟན་པའི་ས་གཞི་ལ། །མོས་གུས་དཔག་བསམ་ལྗོན་ཤིང

༄༅། །ཨང་ཕྱོགས་རིགས་མེད་པའི་ཐོས་བསམ་བྱས། །ཐེ་ཚོམ་བློ་ཡི་ཕུགས་ཐག་བཅད། །ཆོས་དང་ཆོས་མིན་བླང་དོར་ཤེས། །མདུན་མའི་རྩེ་མོ

Homage to the Guru. To Padmasambhava, who knows the three times, and Pema Lingpa, I offer them as an ornament on the crown of my head. I, the yogi of the degenerate age, Pema Lingpa, though I have no provisional meaning to give, I rely on the definitive meaning that benefits others. You fortunate followers and students, keep this in your minds without distraction! Although the natural state of the primordial mind is unerring from the beginning, look at the root of where the essence of delusion or non-delusion arises! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has no source from the beginning, look at the original ground of the effort of arising and accomplishing! Although the natural state of the primordial mind is without a location from the beginning, look at the essence of the one who stays and grasps at the thought of staying! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has no coming or going from the beginning, look at who it is that goes and has the thought of going! Although the natural state of the primordial mind is empty from the beginning, look at whether the essence of appearance at the time of emptiness is pervasive or not!

<leaf-break/>

Cut the deep cord of the delusion of the afflictions from the very beginning. By meditating on the stainless <term>samadhi</term>, realize the ultimate realization at the end. If you accomplish the great goal, you will hold your own ground. You will remain in the unerring meaning. You will attain immeasurable happiness. You will find the seven riches of the noble ones. When those coarse and heavy conceptual thoughts are exhausted in the non-referential state of their own place, strive with precise and meticulous diligence. No matter what proliferation of words and meanings arises, do not fall under the power of grasping, but look at the mind and let it be clear. Let it rest vividly in the state of calm abiding. When the grasping of that which has stains is exhausted, the Clear Light of Superior Insight will dawn from within. The primordial meaning is without movement or agitation. Having found it for yourself, recognize your own nature. The excellent result is already accomplished. It is the peaceful realm of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>expanse of reality</gloss>. It is staying on the ground of a Buddha. From the very state of the unborn <term>dharmakaya</term>, it is nothing other than the Great Expanse.

<leaf-break/>

Mothers, children, and relatives are all spurred by their own individual karma. When death gradually occurs, the suffering of others becomes my own. Who can bear the suffering of death? When the benefit of one's karma is exhausted, even the Buddhas of the three times must depart when their work for beings is finished. What power to stay do any beings of the three realms have? When struck by the demon of the Lord of Death, even a <term>chakravartin</term> <gloss>universal monarch</gloss> must go, leaving his kingdom behind. Even the lineage of lords and officials must go, leaving their castles and estates behind. Even wealthy householders must go, leaving their wealth and possessions behind. Even if one has many children and relatives, one must go all alone. Just as others have departed for the sake of the next life, there is no certainty as to when it will be my turn. Keep that thought in your mind and cast away your current busyness! There is no benefit in doing it. These eight worldly concerns are like the ripples on flowing water.

(3)中論八不表解

不生：萬法無生。何以故？世間眼現見故。如劫初穀不生，何以故？離劫初穀，今穀不可得。若離劫初穀有今穀者，則應有生，而實不爾，是故不生。

不滅：劫初穀不滅。何以故？若滅，今不應有穀，而實有穀，是故不滅。

不常：萬物不常。如穀生芽時，種則變壞，是故不常。

不斷：萬物不斷。如從穀有芽，是故不斷，若斷不應相續。

不一：萬物不一。如穀不作芽、芽不作穀。若是一，而實不爾，是故不一。

不異：萬物不異。若異者何故分別穀芽、穀莖、穀葉，不說樹芽、樹莖、樹葉，是故不異。

不來：萬物不來。如穀中芽，無所從來。若來者，芽應從餘處來，如鳥來棲樹，而實不爾，是故不來。

不出：萬物不出。若有出，應見芽從穀出，如蛇從穴出，而實不爾，是故不出。

No duality: No "existence of grasper and grasped."
Existence of this non-existence: Existence of the "non-existence of grasper and grasped."
These two as non-dual are called empty characteristics.

Also, explanations generally hold that all three modes of karma are complete. Separately, "bowing the head" belongs to the body, and "taking refuge in the life-source" is the mind. Among the three modes of karma, the mental mode is the most important. As is known, if a sage stirs anger, he can cause the people of three kingdoms to die. 
The second part, regarding the object of reverence, also has two sections. The first, "exhausting the ten directions," clarifies the extent of the object of reverence. There are two meanings here: 
1. It does not mean just taking refuge in the Three Jewels of one direction, but rather an intent to exhaust the ten directions in equal reverence. 
2. Within the ten directions, it does not mean just taking refuge in one world-system after another, but rather that in each place of the ten directions, one exhausts the infinite worlds and all the Three Jewels of those regions. Why is this so? To manifest that the Three Jewels are omnipresent, that the heart is vast, to distinguish this from the Lesser Vehicle, and as a mark for this treatise. Thus, "exhausting the ten directions." 
The second part identifies the Three Jewels that are revered, containing three sections. The first three phrases explain the Buddha Jewel. The next three phrases explain the Dharma Jewel. <margin>183</margin>

This matter is extremely profound, and whoever merits to understand it will grasp a great mystery concerning the nature of souls. Know that we shall explain one matter here, for it is known that all souls were contained within the first man <term>Adam ha-Rishon</term> <gloss>the First Man/Adam</gloss> before he sinned. After he sinned, they were separated from him, and each and every soul <unclear>is attached</unclear>.

Now, our sages of blessed memory said regarding the verse in Job, "Indeed, God does all these things, twice, three times with a man" <note>Job 33:29</note>, that the soul does not come in transmigration <term>gilgul</term> <gloss>reincarnation/cycle of rebirth</gloss> more than three times. If it is not rectified then, it is cut off, Heaven forbid. However, know that this applies specifically to a soul alone. But if a part of it was rectified and it returned a second time and another part was rectified, and it returned a third time and the whole of it was rectified, then it does not come again in transmigration, for it is already completed. However, if in these three times it was not rectified at all, then it is cut off, Heaven forbid.

<margin>185</margin>

Here we shall explain the matter of transmigration <term>gilgul</term> <gloss>reincarnation</gloss>, about which the commentators of blessed memory struggled: How is it possible that souls come in transmigration, when our sages of blessed memory have said that in the time to come all bodies will rise in the resurrection of the dead <term>techiyat ha-metim</term> <gloss>resurrection of the dead</gloss>? If one soul comes into several bodies, which one of them will rise at the resurrection? If you say the last one, then what will become of the first ones? And if you say all of them will rise, then to whom among them will the soul belong? 

Know that, in truth, the matter is as we have written: every soul possesses many sparks <term>nitzotzot</term> <gloss>divine sparks</gloss>, and each spark clothes itself in one body. Each and every spark requires rectification on its own, and that spark which was rectified in that body is the one that will rise with it at the time of the resurrection. That spark which was not rectified will return in transmigration in another body until it is rectified. Thus, it is found that all the bodies will rise, and each and every one will take its portion of the soul according to what was rectified within it. This is the mystery of the verse "and they shall eat its portion" <note>referencing the idea that each body receives its sustenance from its part of the soul</note>, for every body will eat and take its portion of the soul. 

This is the mystery of what our sages of blessed memory said, that in the time to come, every righteous person will have three hundred and ten worlds, according to the numerical value of "substance" <term>yesh</term> <gloss>existence/substance</gloss>, as it is said: "To endow those who love Me with substance <term>yesh</term>, and I will fill their treasuries" <note>Proverbs 8:21</note>. 

Know that the matter is that every soul is comprised of six hundred and thirteen limbs <term>taryag evarim</term> <gloss>the 613 commandments corresponding to the limbs of the soul</gloss>, and each limb is divided into many sparks. Each and every spark is a full world unto itself, and each and every spark requires rectification on its own. That spark which was rectified in that body is the one that will rise with it at the time of the resurrection. This is the mystery of "to endow those who love Me with substance," for each and every spark is a full world according to the numerical value of <term>yesh</term>. This is the mystery of what our sages of blessed memory said, that all Israel has a share in the world to come, as it is said: "And your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever" <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>.

If it is not rectified then, it is cut off, Heaven forbid. However, know that this applies specifically to a soul alone. But if a part of it was rectified and it returned a second time and another part was rectified, and it returned a third time and the whole of it was rectified, then it does not come again in transmigration, for it is already completed. However, if in these three times it was not rectified at all, then it is cut off, Heaven forbid.

<summary>This page addresses the kabbalistic mechanism of reincarnation, explaining how divine sparks within a soul are rectified across multiple bodies and how each spark's individual rectification ensures its inclusion in the resurrection of the dead.</summary>

56

...having described the position up to the Great Power <note><term>Mahashakti</term></note> in that order. And below that, O Goddess, in the middle of the lunar mandala, consider the triangle. In that is the digit that is eternal. Inside that is the <term>Kutila</term>, the seventeenth digit called <term>Nirvana</term>. According to this statement, the position of the <term>Ama</term> digit and others is within the triangle inside the lunar mandala. The <term>Guru</term>, however, is situated below that or above the Inner Self. If it is asked: "The <term>Kankalamalini</term> text says the <term>Guru</term> is above the Inner Self, so how is it said that the <term>Guru</term> is above the <term>Hamsa</term>?" The answer is that <term>Hamsa</term> and the Inner Self are identical. Thus, the meditation on the <term>Guru</term> in the <term>Kankalamalini Tantra</term> is: "The supreme Inner Self situated in the middle of the thousand-petaled lotus. Above it, in the middle of the sound and the point <note><term>Nada-Bindu</term></note>, on the brilliant throne, meditate on your constant <term>Guru</term>..." and so on. Similarly, elsewhere: "On the <term>Hamsa</term> seat, meditate on your own <term>Guru</term> of the form of Shiva, who is the mantra..." and so on. Likewise, in the <term>Annada Kalpa</term>: "In the head-lotus, the white thousand-petaled one, in the filaments, on the seat of the birds <note>referring to the Hamsa</note>, meditate on your own <term>Guru</term> who is the form of the Supreme Shiva." Upon examination of these statements, a difference between the <term>Hamsa</term> and the Inner Self appears. Thus, by "your own <term>Guru</term> of the form of the Supreme Shiva," one should understand that the Supreme Shiva is the <term>Guru</term>. The statement "Starting with the thousand-petaled lotus, in its middle is a triangle of lightning-form; in its middle are two points, the immutable <term>Visarga</term>; in that void space is the Shiva called the Supreme" indicates the position of the Supreme Shiva in the middle of the triangle. According to the differences in those views, this is the position of the <term>Guru</term> within the triangle of the pericarp of the twelve-petaled lotus <note>usually associated with the Heart Chakra, but here noted as a point of reference for the head</note> which is not different from the thousand-petaled lotus, as clarified in the <term>Paduka Panchaka Stotra</term>. It does not indicate the position of the <term>Guru</term> in the triangle of the thousand-petaled lotus pericarp. It is situated below the central triangle, in the other triangle, in that form. Otherwise, it would contradict the <term>Kankalamalini Tantra</term>. "He is the Lord of all" means here in the pericarp, the Lord of all resides. If the position of the Supreme Shiva is stated here, why is the position of the Lord of all mentioned again?

<summary>This page clarifies the positions of the Guru, the Supreme Shiva, and the Inner Self within the thousand-petaled lotus, navigating apparent contradictions in different tantric texts.</summary>

->एकविंशतिपटलः । ४८<-

सुचारुदशनां नित्यां पीनोन्नतपयोधराम् ।
विभङ्गस्थानसंस्थानां महिषासुरमर्दिनीम् ॥ २५ ॥
मृणालायतसंस्पर्शां दशबाहुसमन्विताम् ।
विशूलं दक्षिणेध्येयं खड्गं चक्रं च क्रमात् ॥ २६ ॥
तीक्ष्णां वामतथाशक्तिं बाहुदण्डे विभ्रतीम् ।
खेटकं पूर्णचापञ्च पाशमङ्कुशमुद्रिताम् ॥ २७ ॥
घण्टां वापरमं वापि वामतः सन्निवेशयेत् ।
रक्तचन्दनसिक्ताङ्गीं रक्ताम्बरपरिच्छदाम् ॥ २८ ॥
सिंहस्थां परमेशानीं ब्रह्मविष्णुशिवार्चिताम् ।
प्रेतस्थाञ्च महामायां रक्तपद्मासन स्थिताम् ॥ २९ ॥
सिंहस्थाञ्च तथा दुर्गां ध्यायेत् परममोक्षदाम् ।
शिवः प्रेतोमहादेवो ब्रह्मासोहितपङ्कजः ॥ ३० ॥
विष्णुः सिंह इति ख्यातः वाहनानिमहौजसः ।
स्वमूर्त्त्यावाहनं नैव तेषां देवि प्रयुज्यते ॥ ३१ ॥
तत्तन्मूर्त्त्यन्तरं कृत्वावाहनत्वं गतास्त्वयः ।
शिवप्रेते कदाचित्स्यात्कदाचिद्रक्तपङ्कजे ॥ ३२ ॥
कदाचित्केशरपृष्ठे वसते परमेश्वरि ।
कामकाले शिवप्रेते वसतेसिंहवाहिनी ॥ ३३ ॥
अस्यामहिषमहिष्याः प्रियं सखीगणं शृणु ॥ ३४ ॥

इति श्रीकामिविलास-तन्त्रेएकविंशतिपटलः समाप्तः ।

एषाविद्या महाविद्या चतुर्वर्ग फलप्रदा ।
मायाबीजं समुद्धृत्य तथान्ते वह्निवल्लभा ॥ ८ ॥
एषातवत्तरीविद्या मर्हिन्यादोषवर्जिता ।
ह्रीं दुर्गे तत्तरं मन्त्रं चतुर्वर्ग प्रदायकम् ॥ ९ ॥
ह्रीं दुर्गे रक्षणि पदं नमइत्यच्चरं ततः ।
मायाबीजं समुद्धृत्य वह्निजाया परं तथा ॥ १० ॥
चतुईशाक्षरीविद्या सर्वदोषविवर्जिता ।
ह्रीं दुर्गे तत्तरं मन्त्रं चतुर्वर्गप्रदायकम् ॥ ११ ॥

शब्दस्य पाततो घण्टा गन्धाद्यैः परिपूजिता ॥ १२ ॥
तदधः संस्थितं नित्यं अङ्कुशं उन्मनीमयम् ।
तदधः संस्थितं पाशं सिद्धिदं परिच्छदम् ॥ १३ ॥
चापञ्च तदधो देवि तदधः खेटकं परम् ।
इति ते कथितं मर्वं जम्बुभारतसम्मतम् ॥ १४ ॥
विपरीतं यतन्यायं अन्यवर्णस्य मन्त्रणम् ।
कामबीजं त्रिशूलञ्च खङ्गं मायां तथैव च ॥ १५ ॥
चक्रं कूर्चं महेशानि वाणं वाग्भवमीरितम् ।
शक्त्यस्त्रञ्च श्रियाबीजं वामहस्तेऽवतारितम् ॥ १६ ॥
खेटकं माम्नाय बीजं चापमङ्कुशमीरितम् ।
अङ्कुशञ्च तथापाशं कन्दर्पराजमीरितम् ॥ १७ ॥
याघण्टा चञ्चला लाङ्गि सिद्धिस्वरूपिणी ।
नित्याश्रीकमलाबीजरूपिणी सिद्धिदायिनी ॥ १८ ॥
परञ्च तथा देवि माकरध्वजमीरितम् ।
विपरीतमतं देवि भक्ताति परिकीर्त्तितम् ॥ १९ ॥
अथान्यात्संप्रवक्ष्यामिगिरिशे नगनन्दिने ।
वामबाहोरूद्धेगे त्रिशूलं त्रिगुणात्मकम् ॥ २० ॥
तदधश्च तथा खङ्गं चक्रञ्च तदधः क्रमात् ।
तदधस्तथावाणञ्च शक्तिञ्च तदधः क्रमात् ॥ २१ ॥
दक्षबाहोरूद्धभागे खेटकं दीप्यते प्रिये ।
तदधः पूर्णं चापञ्च तदधः पाशमङ्कुशम् ॥ २२ ॥
तदधश्च तथा घण्टां परशुं परमाद्भुतम् ।
विपरीतमिदं प्रोक्तं भक्ताति नगनन्दिनी ॥ २३ ॥
अतःपरं प्रवक्ष्यामि विपरीतं यथोचितम् ।
यस्य विज्ञानमात्रेण शिवतुल्यो भवेन्नरः ॥ २४ ॥
वामबाहोरूद्धभागे शक्तिं परमशोभनाम् ।
तदधस्तथावाणञ्च तदधश्चक्रमेव च ॥ २५ ॥

दुर्गापञ्चाक्षरं मन्त्रं ब्रह्मोपेन्द्रादिपूजितम् ।
त्वं दुर्गेरक्षणिपदं जपात् सिद्धिदायकम् ॥ १२ ॥
ह्रीं दुर्गेरक्षणिह्रूं नम इत्यक्षरं ततः ।
मायाबीजं समुद्धृत्य वह्निजायापदेरतः ॥ १३ ॥
चतुर्दशाक्षरोविद्या सर्वदोषविवर्जिता ।
आद्यन्ते प्रणवं माया यदि स्याद्वर्णिनि ॥ १४ ॥
तदैषा षोडशीविद्या सर्वकामफलप्रदा ।
षोडशी मन्त्रविज्ञानं विना यौवननन्दिनि ॥ १५ ॥
यत्किञ्चित् क्रियतेकर्म निष्फलं पूजनादिकं ।
तस्मादवश्यं ज्ञातव्यं मन्त्रिण्याः षोडशाक्षरं ॥ १६ ॥
यथोक्तं सर्वतन्त्रेषु अधुना कथयामिति ।

हास्खाणित्चरगेंदुगेंदु ह्रीं ॥

दशाक्षर मिदं प्रोक्तं विपरीतं विलोमकं ॥ १७ ॥
विपरीत परिज्ञानात् शीघ्रसिद्धिः प्रजायते ।
अज्ञानादिपरोतस्य न सिद्धिर्जायते कलौ ॥ १८ ॥
एवं सर्वत्र वोद्धव्यं दशविद्यासुसुन्दरि ।
लक्षणाकोटि मन्त्रेषु शिवमन्त्र तथैव च ॥ १९ ॥
प्रकृतस्यानुलोमञ्च विपरीतं विलोमकं ।
मतान्तरं विपरीतं शृणुष्व प्राणवल्लभे ॥ २० ॥

( ॐ ह्रीं हास्खाणित्चरगेंदुगेंदु ह्रीं ॐ )

त्रयोदशाक्षरं मन्त्रं, विपरितमिदं मतं ।

( ॐ ह्रीं ह्रूं हास्खागेंदुगेंदुणित्चर ह्रूं ह्रीं ॐ )

विपरीतमिदं मन्त्रं दुर्गायाः षोडशाक्षरं ॥ २१ ॥
गेंदुगेंदुक्षरं मन्त्रं सर्वकामफलप्रदं ।

"गेंदुगेंदुॐ"

इति पञ्चाक्षरं मन्त्रं सर्वतन्त्रसुगोपितं ॥ २२ ॥
यत्रयत्रविनिर्दिष्टं तत्रैव परिकल्प्यते ।
मतान्तरं विपरीतं शृणुष्व प्राणवल्लभे ॥ २३ ॥
